Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 1:

(p-58)(4 Sūrat al-Nisā')

Madaniyyah (Medinan), and it has one hundred and seventy-five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind!﴾ This is an address encompassing the children of Adam. ﴿Be mindful of your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾ — that is Adam. ﴿And from it He created its mate﴾ — a conjunction with "created you," meaning: He created you from a single person, and from him He created your mother Ḥawwā' from one of his ribs; or it is elided, its estimated meaning being "from a single soul He created, and from it He created its mate," and this is a confirmation of their creation from a single soul. ﴿And from the two of them He scattered many men and women﴾ — an explanation of the manner of their procreation from the two of them. The meaning is: He spread from that soul and the mate created from it many sons and daughters. He suffices with describing the men as many instead of describing the women with it, since wisdom requires that they be more numerous. He mentioned "many" in the sense of the plural, and He linked the command to be mindful [of God] to this narrative because of what it contains of indication of the overpowering might that deserves to be feared, and the dazzling blessing that necessitates obedience to the One who bestowed it; or because its purpose is to pave the way for the command to be mindful [of God] regarding the rights of the people of one's household and of one's kind, as the verses that follow indicate. It is also read "wa-khāliqu" and "wa-bāththu," with an elided subject, its estimated form being "wa-huwa khāliqun wa-bāththun" (and He is the Creator and the Scatterer). ﴿And be mindful of Allah, through whom you ask one another﴾ — that is, some of you ask others, saying, "I ask you by Allah." Its origin is "tatasā'alūna," and the second tā' was assimilated into the sīn. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read it with the tā' omitted.

﴿And the wombs﴾ — in the accusative, a conjunction with the place of the prepositional phrase, as in your saying: "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr," or governed by "Allah," meaning: be mindful of Allah and be mindful of the wombs, so maintain them and do not sever them. Ḥamzah read it in the genitive, as a conjunction with the pronoun in the genitive, and this is weak because it is like part of the word. It is also read in the nominative, as an elided-predicate subject, its estimated form being "and the wombs are likewise," that is, among what is to be feared or by which one asks. By joining the wombs to His noble Name, He, glorified and exalted, has alerted that their connection has a place with Him.

And from him, upon him be prayer and peace: "The womb is suspended from the Throne, saying: Whoever joins me, Allah joins him, and whoever severs me, Allah severs him."

﴿Indeed Allah is ever watchful over you﴾ — a guardian, one who observes.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 2:

﴿And give the orphans their property﴾, i.e., when they reach maturity. "Orphans" (al-yatama) is the plural of yatim, who is one whose father has died, from al-yutm (yutm), which means being alone (al-infirad).

From this comes the expression "a unique pearl" (al-durrah al-yatimah). It is either that, since it has come to function as a noun, like faris (horseman) and sahib (companion), it was pluralized as yata'im and then transposed to yatama, or that it was pluralized as yutma, like asra (captives), because it belongs to the category of calamities (al-afat). Then yutma was pluralized as yatama, like asra and asara (captives). Etymology requires that it apply to both the young and the old, but usage has restricted it to those who have not reached maturity. Its occurrence in the verse is either for one who has reached maturity, according to the original sense, or by extension, because their time of being young is recent, urging that one should hand over their property to them at the very beginning of their maturity, before this designation departs from them, if sound judgment is perceived in them. For this reason he commanded that they be tested while they are young, or while they have not yet reached maturity, and the ruling is restricted. So it is as if he said:

"and give it to them when they reach maturity." The first interpretation is supported by what has been narrated: "A man from Ghatafan had a great deal of wealth belonging to his nephew, an orphan. When the nephew reached maturity, he asked him for the wealth, but he refused, so this verse was revealed. When the uncle heard it, he said: 'We obey God and His Messenger; we seek refuge in God from the great sin.'"

﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾: do not exchange the unlawful from their property for the lawful from your property. Or the bad thing is the wasting of their property in exchange for the good thing, which is preserving it. It is said: do not take the superior from their property and give the inferior in its place; this is a substitution but not an exchange.

﴿And do not devour their property together with your property﴾: do not consume it combined with your property, i.e., do not spend the two together or treat them as equal. This one is lawful and that one is unlawful. This applies to what exceeds the amount of his wage, according to His words, Exalted is He: "let him eat in reasonable manner" (4:6). ﴿Indeed, it﴾: the pronoun refers to the eating. ﴿is a great sin﴾: a grave offense. It is also read as ḥawban, which is a verbal noun of ḥāba ḥawban and ḥābān, like qāla qawlan and qālan.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 3:

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ That is: if you fear that you will not be just regarding the orphan women when you marry them, then marry what seems good to you of other than them. For a man would find an orphan girl who has wealth and beauty, and he would marry her out of greed for her, so that he might end up with a number of them and be unable to fulfil their rights. Or, if you fear that you will not be just regarding the rights of the orphans, and so you scruple about them, then fear likewise that you will not be just among women, and marry an amount that you can fulfil the right of. For one who scrupulates about sin should scrupulate about all sins. This is according to what is related: "When the matter of orphans became grave, they scrupulated about guardianship over them, but they did not scruple about multiplying wives and neglecting them, so this was revealed."

It was said: They used to scruple about guardianship over orphans but did not scruple about fornication. So it was said to them: if you fear that you will not be just regarding the matter of orphans, then fear fornication, and marry what is lawful for you.

He expressed them with "mā" (what) either by considering the attribute, or by treating them as the likes of non-rational beings because of the deficiency of their intellect. Its parallel is: "or what your right hands possess." It has also been read "tuqsitū" with a fathah on the ta', with "lā" taken as superfluous, meaning: if you fear that you will deviate (from justice).

﴿Two, and three, and four﴾ are formed as distributive numbers (ma'dūlah) from repeated numbers, namely: two by two, three by three, and four by four. They are not declinable (ghayr munṣarifah) on account of the ʿadl (deviation of form) and the ṣifah (attributive quality), for they were formed as attributes, although their roots were not formed for that purpose. It has also been said that it is due to the repetition of the ʿadl, for they are deviated (from their base form) with regard to both the attribute and the repetition. They are in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) from the subject of ṭāba. Their meaning is the permission for every marrying man who wishes to combine several wives to marry whatever number of the stated amount he wishes, whether they are equal or different in it, as in your saying: "Divide this purse two dirhams two dirhams, and three three," and if they were stated singly the meaning would be permission to combine these numbers without distribution; and if they were stated with "aw" (or), the permission to differ in number would be lost.

﴿And if you fear that you will not be just﴾ among these numbers also. ﴿then one﴾ That is: choose or marry one wife and leave off combining. It has also been read with a nominative (fa-wāḥidatun), as the subject of an omitted verb or as a predicate, its estimate being: "then one suffices you," or "then the one who suffices is one."

﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾ He equated the single wife from among the wives with a number of concubines, because of the lightness of their maintenance and the non-obligation of equal division among them. ﴿That﴾ i.e., limiting oneself to them, or choosing one wife, or taking concubines. ﴿Is nearer that you will not be unjust﴾ nearer than that you will not incline (away from justice). It is said: "ʿāla al-mīzān" when the scale tilts, and "ʿāla al-ḥākim" when the judge acts unjustly; and ʿawl al-farīḍah is the deviation from the limit of the stated shares. It has been interpreted as "that you will not have many dependents," taking it from "ʿāla al-rajul ʿiyālahu yaʿūluhum" when he supports them, so the abundance of dependents is expressed by the abundance of maintenance, by way of metonymy. This is supported by the reading "an lā taʿīlū," from "aʿāla al-rajul" when his dependents increase. Perhaps the intended meaning of the dependents is the wives; and if the children are intended, then it is because concubinage is a likely cause of fewer children in comparison with marriage, since withdrawal (ʿazl) is permissible in it, just as marrying one is compared with marrying four.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 4:**

﴿And give the women their *sadaqat* (dower)﴾: their *muhur* (marriage gifts, singular *mahr*). It is read with a *fatha* on the *sad* and a sukun on the *dal* as a lightened form, and with a *damma* on the *sad* and a sukun on the *dal*, as the plural of *sadaqah*, like *ghurfah*. It is also read with both vowelled with a *damma*, in the singular, which is the heavier form of *sadaqah*, like *zulmah* as *zulmah*. ﴿*Nihlah*﴾: that is, a gift. One says *nahalahu kadha nihlatan wa nahlan* when one gives him such-and-such freely, with good will and without expecting a return. Whoever explains it as an obligatory portion (*fari𝑑ah*) or similar has considered the implied meaning of the verse, not the lexical meaning of the word. It is in the accusative either as a verbal noun, since it carries the sense of giving (*itaʾ*), or as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the *waw* (of the plural verb), or of *al-sadaqat*, meaning: give them their dowers while giving freely, or as a gift. It has been said that the meaning is "a gift from God and a bounty from Him to them," so it is a state of *al-sadaqat*. It has also been said that it means "a religious obligation" (*diyanah*), from the expression *intahala fulan kadha* when he adopted it as his religion, and that it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) or a state of *al-sadaqat*, meaning: a debt from God Most High, which He legislated. The address is to the husbands. It has also been said that it is addressed to the guardians, because they used to take the dowers of those under their guardianship.

﴿And if they give you willingly any part of it, [then] consume it, [as] satisfying and wholesome﴾: the pronoun refers to the dower (*sadaq*), by treating it according to its meaning, or it operates like a demonstrative noun, as in the verse of Ru'bah:

*"As if on the skin is the spreading of leprosy's patches (*tawlia al-buhaq*)"*

When he was asked about it, he said: "I meant, as if that were..." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the giving (*itaʾ*). *Nafsan* is a specifying accusative (*tamyiz*) to explain the genus, and for that reason it is singular. The meaning is: "If they give you something of the dower with good will." However, the essential element is made good will, for emphasis. It is governed by *ʿan* because it implies the sense of turning aside (*tajafi*) and overlooking (*tajawuz*). He said *minhu* (of it) to encourage them to give away little of what is given. ﴿*Fakuluhu hanian mariʾan*﴾: so take it and spend it, lawfully, without any consequence. *Al-hanii* and *al-mariʾ* are two adjectives from *hanaʾa al-taʿam* and *mara'a* when food goes down smoothly without choking. They are put in place of their verbal nouns, or the verbal noun is described by them, or they are made circumstantial states of the pronoun. It has been said that *al-hanii* is what a person enjoys, and *al-mariʾ* is what has a praiseworthy outcome.

It is related: "Some people used to feel sinful that one of them should accept anything from his wife of what he had given her as dower. So this verse was revealed."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 5:

﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾ is a prohibition addressed to the guardians (awliya') against handing over their property to those who lack sound judgment (rushd), so that they squander it. He attributed the property to the guardians because it is under their control and in their charge, and this fits the preceding and following verses. It has also been said that it is a prohibition addressed to everyone against deliberately giving to his wife and children the wealth that Allah has entrusted to him, and then sitting back to look at their hands. He called them foolish (sufaha') to belittle their intellects and to censure the placing of them in charge of themselves (qiwaman 'ala anfusihim). This is more fitting with His words: ﴿which Allah has made for you a means of support (qiyaman)﴾, meaning the things by which you stand firm and are sustained. According to the first interpretation, it is taken to mean that they are of the kind of things that Allah has made a means of support for you, and what is used for support is called qiyam by way of emphasis. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "qiyaman" (qiyaman), with the same meaning, like 'iwadh (refuge) and 'iyadh (in the sense of seeking refuge). It is also read "qawaman" (qawaman), which means that by which one is supported.

﴿And provide for them from it and clothe them﴾: make it a source of their provision and clothing, by trading with it and obtaining from its profit what they need. ﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾: a fair promise by which their souls are comforted. The ma'ruf (what is good and recognized) is what the Shari'ah or reason recognizes as good, and the munkar (what is evil and rejected) is what either of them rejects as ugly.

Test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Test them beforehand, by following up their circumstances in soundness of religion and the ability to manage property and act wisely, by entrusting to them the preliminaries of a contract. And from Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, [the testing is] by handing over to them what they can dispose of.

﴿Until, when they reach marriageable age﴾: until they reach the limit of puberty, by having a wet dream, or by completing fifteen years of age according to us, on the basis of his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "When the child completes fifteen years, what is his and what is against him is recorded, and the prescribed punishments are applied to him."

﴿And eighteen﴾ according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. "Reaching marriage" is a metonymy for puberty, because he is fit for marriage according to him. ﴿If you perceive in them maturity﴾, that is, if you sense in them maturity. It has also been read as "aḥastum," with the same meaning as "aḥsastum." ﴿Then hand over to them their property﴾ without delay after the limit of puberty. The structure of the verse is that the conditional "in" (if) is the answer to "idha" (when), which carries the meaning of a condition, and the whole clause is the end point of the testing. It is as if it were said: "Test the orphans until the time of their puberty and their becoming entitled to having their property handed over to them, on condition that maturity is perceived in them." This is evidence that property is not handed over to them unless maturity has been perceived in them. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: if they have exceeded the age of puberty by seven years, which is a period considered significant in the change of conditions, since the child distinguishes after it and is commanded to worship, the property is handed over to him even if maturity has not been perceived in him.

﴿And do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, [fearing] that they will grow up﴾, that is, wasteful and hasty, anticipating their growing up; or, [fearing] your extravagance and haste in [consuming] it before they grow up. ﴿And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain﴾ from consuming it. ﴿And whoever is poor, let him eat in an reasonable manner﴾, according to his need and the wage of his labor. The wording "abstaining" and "eating in a reasonable manner" indicates that the guardian has a right to the child's property. From him, upon him be prayers and peace: "A man said to him, 'I have an orphan in my custody; may I eat from his property?' He said: 'Eat in a reasonable manner, without accumulating property, and without protecting your property with his property.'"

The placing of this division after His saying "and do not consume it" indicates that it is a prohibition for the guardians to take and spend on themselves the property of orphans. ﴿So when you hand over to them their property, then have witnesses against them that they have received it﴾, for that is more protective against accusation and further from dispute. The obligation of guarantee, and its apparent meaning, indicates that the custodian is not believed in his claim except with evidence. This is our preferred position, and it is the position of Malik, in contrast to Abu Hanifa. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾, the one who calls to account. So do not oppose what you have been commanded, and do not exceed what has been set as limits for you.

For the men there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave, and for the women there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave. He means by them those who inherit by kinship. "Of what little or much of it" is a substitute (badal) for "of what they leave," with the governing verb repeated. "A share ordained" (nasiban mafrudan) is in the accusative as an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid), like His saying, "an obligation from God" (fari'atan min Allah), or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), since the meaning is: a share has been established for them as ordained; or it is in the accusative of specification (ikhtisas), in the sense of "I mean a share fixed and obligatory for them." In this is evidence that if an heir turns away from his share, his right does not lapse.

It was narrated: "That Aws ibn al-Samit al-Ansari died leaving his wife Umm Kuhha and three daughters. His two cousins, Suwayd and 'Urfuta, or Qatada and 'Urfuja, took his inheritance from them, according to the custom of the Jahiliyya, for they did not give inheritance to women and children, and they would say: 'Only one who fights and defends the domain inherits.' Umm Kuhha came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at the Mosque of al-Fadikh and complained to him. He said: 'Return until I see what God brings about.' Then the verse was revealed, and he sent to them both: 'Do not divide anything from the property of Aws, for God has appointed a share for them, and has not explained it until He explains it.' Then it was revealed: 'God enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, the equal of the portion of two females' (4:11), so He gave Umm Kuhha the eighth and the daughters two-thirds, and the remainder to the two cousins." This is evidence for the permissibility of delaying an explanation beyond the time of the address.

And when the division takes place, the near relatives who do not inherit, and the orphans and the needy, are present; so provide for them from it, give them something from what is divided, to comfort their hearts and as charity toward them. This is a command of recommendation (amr nadb) for the adult heirs. It has been said that it is a command of obligation, and then scholars differed about its abrogation (naskh). The pronoun refers to "what they leave," or to what the division implies. "And speak to them a kind word": that is, they should pray for them, and belittle what they have given them, and not reproach them for it.

﴿And let those fear [Allah] who, if they were to leave behind them weak offspring, would fear for them﴾. [The phrase] "let those fear" is a command to the executors (al-awsiya') that they should fear God, the Exalted, and be mindful of Him in the matter of orphans, so that they treat them as they would like their own weak offspring to be treated after their death. Or it is addressed to those present at the bedside of a sick person at the time of making a bequest, that they should fear their Lord. Or it means that they should fear for the children of the sick person and feel compassion for them, as they feel compassion for their own children, so that they do not allow him to harm them by diverting the wealth away from them. Or it is addressed to the heirs, [urging them] to show compassion toward the weak relatives, orphans and needy who are present at the division of the estate, imagining that if they were their own children and were left behind weak like them, would they permit their being deprived? Or it is addressed to those making bequests, that they should consider the heirs and not be extravagant in the bequest, even if it is within the permitted portion.

The relative clause (sila) is attached to "those" (alladhina), in the sense that: "and let those fear whose condition and attribute is that, if they were about to leave behind weak offspring, they would fear the loss of them." The placing of the command upon this condition indicates its purpose and its rationale. It also urges mercy, and that one should love for the children of others what one loves for one's own children, and it is a warning to the one who opposes this by [pointing to] the condition of his own children.

﴿So let them be mindful of Allah and let them speak words of rectitude﴾. He commanded them to have taqwa (God-consciousness), which is the ultimate goal of fear, after He had commanded them to fear, observing both the beginning and the end, since the first is of no benefit without the second. Then He commanded them to speak to the orphans the same words they would speak to their own children, with compassion and good manners. Or [it means] to speak to the sick person words that restrain him from extravagance in the bequest and from depriving the heirs, and remind him of repentance and the testimony of faith. Or [it means] to speak to those present at the division a gracious excuse and a good promise. Or [it means] that they should state in the bequest only what does not lead to exceeding the one-third and depriving the heirs.

Surely those who consume the property of orphans wrongfully, being wrongdoers, or in a manner that amounts to wrongdoing. They are only consuming fire into their bellies, the full measure of their bellies, a fire that drags them to the Fire and leads them towards it.

And on the authority of Abu Burda, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah will raise up a people from their graves whose mouths are blazing with fire." It was asked: "Who are they?" He said: "Have you not seen that Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blazing Fire﴾? They will enter a fire, and what a fire!"

Ibn Amir and Ibn Ayyash, on the authority of Asim, read (yaṣlawna) with a dammah on the yāʾ and without shaddah (i.e., yuṣlawna). It was also read with shaddah (yuṣallawna). It is said: ṣalā al-nār, meaning he endured its heat; and ṣallaytuhu, meaning I roasted it; and aṣlaytuhu, and ṣallaytuhu, meaning I cast him into it. And al-saʿīr is a form (faʿīl) in the sense of a passive participle (mafʿūl), from saʿartu al-nār, meaning I kindled the fire when I set it ablaze.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 11:

"Allah enjoins you (yūṣīkum Allāhu)": He commands you and charges you (yaʿhadu ilaykum) concerning your children, regarding the matter of their inheritance. This is a general statement (ijmāl) whose detail follows. "For the male, a portion equal to that of two females": that is, He allots to each male twice the share of a female where both categories are present, so his share is doubled. The specific mention of the male's portion is because the aim is to explain his excellence, and it also alerts that doubling is sufficient for preference, so the females are not entirely deprived, since they share in the category (al-jihah). The meaning is "for the male among them," and it is omitted because it is known.

"If they are women" (fa-in kunna nisāʾan): that is, if the children are purely female, with no male among them. The pronoun is feminine in accordance with the predicate, or in consideration of the children being female (al-mawlūdāt). "Above two" (fawqa thnatayn) is a second predicate, or an adjective for "women," meaning women exceeding two. "Then for them is two-thirds of what the deceased among you left" (fa-lahunna thuluthā mā taraka al-mutawaffā minkum), and the meaning indicates this. "If she is one" (wa-in kānat wāḥidatan), then "for her is half" (fa-lahā al-niṣf): that is, if the female child is one.

Nāfiʿ read it with the nominative (bi-l-raf', al-muqaddar) as "kāna" of complete (al-tāmmah) usage. There is disagreement concerning two daughters. Ibn ʿAbbās (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhumā) said their ruling is the ruling of one, because Allah made two-thirds for those above them. The rest said their ruling is the ruling of those above them, because when Allah clarified that the male's share equals that of two females when a female is with him, which is two-thirds, this required that their fixed share be two-thirds. Then, since that might give the impression that the share increases with an increase in number, He refuted that with His saying: "If they are women above two." This is supported by the fact that a single daughter, when she is entitled to a third along with her brother, then it is more fitting that she be entitled to it along with a sister like her. And two daughters are closer in kinship (amassu raḥiman) than two sisters, and He assigned them two-thirds with His saying, Exalted is He: "For them two-thirds of what he left."

"And for his parents, each one of them": "li-kulli wāḥidin minhumā" is a substitute (badal) from "li-abawayhi," with the repetition of the governing element (bi-takrīr al-ʿāmil). Its benefit is to specify that each of them is entitled to a sixth, and detail after general statement serves as emphasis. "A sixth of what he left, if he has offspring" (lahu walad): male or female. However, the father takes a sixth along with a female by the fixed share (bi-l-farīḍah), and what remains goes to the residuary heirs (dhawī al-furūḍ) also by ʿuṣūbah. "If he has no offspring and his two parents inherit from him alone, then for his mother is a third of what he left." The share of the father is not mentioned because, when He specified that the heirs are only his two parents and fixed the mother's share, it is known that the remainder is for the father. It is as if He said: "So for both of them is what was left in thirds." On this basis, it should be that when one of the spouses is present along with the two parents, the mother has a third of what remains after the spouse's fixed share, as the majority (al-jumhur) said, not a third of the whole estate as Ibn ʿAbbās said, for that would lead to preferring the female over the male who equals her in category and degree, which contradicts the structure of the Sharʿ.

"If he has siblings, then for his mother is a sixth" (fa-in kāna lahu ikhwatun fa-li-ummihi al-sudus): the absolute wording indicates that the siblings reduce her share from a third to a sixth, even though they do not inherit alongside the father. Ibn ʿAbbās (raḍiya Allāhu taʿālā ʿanhumā) reported that they take the sixth from which they have excluded the mother. The majority hold that by "siblings" is meant a number from among those who have siblings, without regard to the three-count requirement, whether they are brothers or sisters. Ibn ʿAbbās (raḍiya Allāhu taʿālā ʿanhumā) said: fewer than three siblings do not exclude the mother from the third, nor do pure sisters, taking the apparent meaning.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "fa-li-ummihi" with a kasrah on the hamzah, following the kasrah that precedes it.

"After a bequest he bequeaths or a debt" (min baʿdi waṣiyyatin yūṣī bihā aw dayn): this relates to all the preceding division of inheritances, meaning these portions are for the heirs after any bequest or debt. The word "aw" (or), which is for permissibility, is used rather than "wa" (and) to indicate that both are equal in obligation and precede the division, whether taken together or separately. He placed the bequest before the debt, though the bequest is later in ruling, because it resembles inheritance and is burdensome to the heirs, and all are encouraged to it, whereas the debt occurs only rarely.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr read "waṣiyyatin" with a fatḥah on the ṣād (yūṣā, reading as above in their reading).

"Your fathers and your sons, you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit": that is, you do not know who is more beneficial to you among those who inherit from you, from your ascendants and descendants, in your present and future life. So be diligent in regard to them in what Allah has commanded you, and do not intend to prefer some and deprive others.

It is related that when one of two who are related by birth is higher in rank than the other in Paradise, he asks that the other be raised to him, and he is raised by his intercession.

"Or from those who bequeath to you among them, or whoever among them has bequeathed, so that He exposes you to reward by carrying out his bequest, or whoever did not bequeath, so that He keeps his wealth for you": this is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) that emphasizes the matter of division or the execution of the bequest.

"An obligation from Allah" (farīḍatan min Allāh): a verbal noun of emphasis (maṣdar muʾakkid), or the verbal noun of "yūṣīkum Allāhu," since it has the meaning of "yaʾmuru" and "yafriḍu ʿalaykum" (commands and imposes upon you).

"Indeed Allah is ever Knowing" of the interests and ranks, "Wise" in what He decrees and ordains.

ۚ And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, then for you is a quarter of what they leave, after any bequest they make or debt. And for them is a quarter of what you leave if you have no child. But if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt.

Commentary: "Ya'nī walad wārith min baṭnihā, aw min ṣulbi banīhā, aw banī banīhā wa-in saflu, dhakaran kāna aw unthā, minkum aw min ghayrikum." That is: a child who inherits, whether from her womb, or from the loins of her sons, or the sons of her sons however low, male or female, from you or from others. "Min ba'di waṣiyyatin yūṣīna bihā aw dayn." And for them is a quarter of what you leave if you have no child, but if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after a bequest you make or debt. He prescribed for the man, by the right of marriage, double what is due to the woman, as in lineage. The same analogy applies to every man and woman who share the same side and degree of kinship, and only the uterine siblings (awlād al-umm), the freed male slave and the freed female slave are excepted from it. The one and the many are equal in the quarter and the eighth.

And if a man (rajul), i.e. the deceased, is inherited (yūrathu), i.e. from whom one inherits (yūrithu minhu man waritha ṣifata rajul), having the quality of a man.

Kalāla is the predicate of kāna, or yūrathu has it as its predicate. Kalāla is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in it, and it refers to one who leaves no child or parent. Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), and what is meant by it is kinship not through a parent or a child. It is permissible that "the man" is the heir and yūrithu refers to the one who bequeaths, and kalāla is one who has neither parent nor child. It is also read yūrithu in the active voice; then "the man" is the deceased, and kalāla admits of the three meanings. On the first, it is a predicate or a circumstantial clause; on the second, an object of purpose; on the third, an object (maf'ūl bihi). Originally it is a verbal noun meaning kalāl (exhaustion), as al-A'shā said:

"So I swore I would not lament her, from kalāla, nor from ḥafā, until I meet Muḥammad."

It was then borrowed for a kinship that is not by offspring (lā bil-ba'ḍiyya), because it is "kalla" (weary) relative to it. Then the inheritor and the one inherited were described by it, in the sense of "one who has kalāla," like your saying "so-and-so is from my kin." Or "a woman" is conjoined to "a man." "And he has" — i.e., and for the man — and the ruling for the man is sufficient without the ruling for the woman, because the conjunction indicates they share in it. "A brother or a sister," i.e. from the mother. This is confirmed by the reading of Ubayy and Sa'd ibn Mālik: "And he has a brother or a sister from the mother." Also, He mentioned at the end of the surah that for two sisters is two-thirds, and for siblings is the whole, and that does not suit uterine siblings. What is determined here is the mother's share, so it is fitting that it be for her children. "For each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that, they are partners in the third." He made equal the male and female in the division, because the connection is by pure femaleness. The implication of the verse is that they do not inherit that with the mother or grandmother, just as they do not inherit with a daughter or son's daughter; this was specified by consensus (ijmā').

"After a bequest that is bequeathed, or a debt, not causing harm" — i.e., not harming his heirs by exceeding the third, or intending harm through the bequest rather than piety, or acknowledging a debt he does not owe. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of yūṣā mentioned in this reading, and what is indicated by his saying yūṣā in the reading of Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir and Ibn 'Ayyāsh from 'Āṣim, where it is passive. "A commandment from Allah": a verbal noun emphasizing, or an object accusative by "not causing harm" as object. It is supported by the reading "ghayra muḍārrin waṣiyyatin" with the genitive, i.e., not harming a bequest from Allah, which is one-third or less, by exceeding it; or a bequest from Him concerning the children, through extravagance in bequest and false acknowledgment. "And Allah is Knowing of the one who causes harm and others; Forbearing, who does not hasten punishment."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 13–14:

"Those" is a reference to the rulings that were set forth concerning the orphans (yatama), the bequests (wasaya), and the inheritances (mawarith). The "limits of Allah" (hudud Allah) are His laws (shara'i'uhu), which are like the bounded limits that may not be crossed. ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and that is the great triumph.﴾

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein; and for him is a humiliating punishment.﴾ The pronoun in "yudkhiluhu" is singular, and the plural "khalidin" is in accordance with the wording and the meaning. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "nudkhiluhu" with the nun, and "khalidin" is a presumptive circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah), like your saying: "I passed by a man with a falcon with him, hunting with it tomorrow." Likewise "khalidan" [in the second verse], and the two are not adjectives (sifatan) for "gardens" and "fire"; otherwise the pronoun would have to be made explicit (iburaz al-damir), because they both apply to other than those to whom they belong.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 15:

Those of your women who commit lewdness (al-fāḥisha), [i.e., who do it]. It is said: "atā al-fāḥisha," "jā'ahā," "ghashiyahā," and "rahiqahā," meaning he committed it. (p-65)

Al-fāḥisha (lewdness) is fornication (al-zinā), because of the increase in its ugliness and abhorrence. ﴿Call to witness against them four of your men﴾, i.e., seek from those who accused them four men from among the believing men to bear witness against them. ﴿If they bear witness, then confine them to the houses﴾, i.e., detain them in the houses and make them a prison for them.

﴿Until death takes them﴾, i.e., death takes their souls, or the angels of death take them. It has been said: this was their punishment in the early days of Islam, and it was abrogated (naskh) by the prescribed penalty (ḥadd). It is possible that what is meant is an injunction to keep them after they have been flogged, so that what happened to them because of going out and exposing themselves to men does not recur. He did not mention the ḥadd, relying on the saying of the Most High: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ (Q. 24:2), or ﴿God makes for them a way﴾ (Q. 4:15), such as the specifying of the ḥadd which releases them from confinement, or marriage which suffices against illicit intercourse.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 16:

﴿And those two of you who commit it⦆ means the adulterous woman and the adulterous man. Ibn Kathir recited "wallaḏāni" (wa-lladhānni) with a doubled nūn and full elongation of the alif, while the rest recited it with a single nūn (lightened, al-takhfif) and without full elongation. ﴿Then hurt them﴾ with rebuke and reproach; it was also said: with reproach and beating. ﴿But if they repent and make amends, then leave them alone﴾ cease harming them, or turn away from them by overlooking and concealing (their fault). ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾ is the reason for the command to turn away and to abandon blame. It was said that this verse preceded the former in revelation, and the punishment for fornication was harm, then confinement, then flogging. It was also said that the former verse concerns lesbians (al-sahhaqat) and this one concerns male homosexuals (al-lawwatin), while "the adulterous woman and the adulterous man" refers to fornicators.

﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah﴾: that is, the acceptance of repentance is as though it were binding upon Allah, by the requirement of His promise, for whoever repents, when He accepts his repentance.

﴿for those who do evil in ignorance﴾: being characterized by it through folly, for committing a sin is foolishness and ignorance. For this reason it has been said: whoever disobeys Allah is ignorant until he desists from his ignorance. ﴿Then they repent soon﴾: from a near time, that is, before the arrival of death, due to His saying: ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾, and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah accepts the repentance of His servant so long as he has not begun the death rattle."

He called it "near" because the span of life is short, due to His saying: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little﴾. Or [it means] before the love of it is instilled into their hearts, so that their hearts are sealed over by it and returning becomes impossible for them. The word "min" (from) is partitive, meaning they repent at any part of the near time, which is the period before the rule of death descends upon them. Or [it means] that they repent before the evil is made attractive to them.

﴿Those, Allah will turn to them﴾: a promise to fulfil what He has promised and what He has prescribed upon Himself by His saying: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah﴾. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾: He knows the sincerity of their repentance. ﴿Wise﴾: and the Wise does not punish the one who repents.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 4, verse 18:**

﴿And repentance (tawbah, turning back to God) is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers.﴾ He equated those who delay repentance until death appears with the wrongdoers (fasaqah) and disbelievers, and those who died in disbelief, in the denial of repentance, for the sake of emphasis on its being disregarded in that state. It is as if he said: the repentance of these and the non-repentance of those are the same. It was said that by "those who do evil" (yaʿmalūna al-sūʾ) are meant the sinners among the believers; by "those who do evil deeds" (yaʿmalūna al-sayyiʾāt) are meant the hypocrites (munafiqūn), because their disbelief and evil deeds are multiplied; and by "those who die" are meant the disbelievers.

﴿Those, We have prepared for them a painful punishment.﴾ This is a confirmation that their repentance is not accepted, and a statement that the punishment that He has prepared for them cannot be thwarted by them whenever He wills. Al-iʿtidād (preparation) means making ready from al-ʿatād (equipment), which is al-ʿuddah (provision). It was said that its origin is aʿdadnā, and the first dal (د) was changed into a tāʾ (ت), so it became aʿtadnā.(p-66)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 19:

﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion.﴾ A man, when he died and had relatives (ʿuṣbah), would throw his garment over his wife and say: "I have more right to her." Then, if he wished, he would marry her with her first bridal gift (ṣadāq); and if he wished, he would marry her to someone else and take her bridal gift; and if he wished, he would prevent her (ʿaḍala) from remarrying so that she would ransom herself with what she had inherited from her husband. So they were forbidden from that. It was also said: "It is not lawful for you to take them by way of inheritance and then marry them while they are unwilling to that, or are compelled to it." Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read kurhan (كُرْهًا) with a ḍammah in its places, and both are two dialects (lughatān).

It was said that with a ḍammah (kurh) it means hardship (al-mashaqqah), and with a fatḥah (kark) it means what one is forced to do.

﴿And do not restrain them (taʿḍulūhunna) in order that you may take away part of what you have given them.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿuṭifa) with "that you inherit," and the "lā" is for emphasizing the negation; that is, do not prevent them from marrying. The root meaning of ʿaḍl is constriction (taḍyīq); it is said: "the hen became constricted with her egg" (ʿaḍalati al-dajājatu bi-bayḍihā).

It was also said: the address is to the husbands, who used to detain women without need or desire until they could inherit from them or until they would ransom themselves (yakhtalaʿna) with their bridal gifts.

It was also said: the sentence is complete at His saying "unwillingly," and then He addressed the husbands and forbade them from ʿaḍl.

﴿Except that they commit a clear immorality (fāḥishah mubayyinah).﴾ Such as disobedience (nushūz), bad conduct toward the spouse, and lack of chastity. The exception is from the most general of general terms, either of the adverbial of time (ẓarf) or of the object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). Its estimate is: "do not restrain them for the sake of ransom except at the time when they commit an immorality," or "do not restrain them for any cause except that they commit an immorality." Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read mubayyinatin here and in al-Aḥzab and al-Ṭalāq with a fatḥah on the yāʾ; the rest read it with a kasrah in them.

﴿And live with them in kindness (bi-al-maʿrūf).﴾ By being just in action and gracious in speech.

﴿And if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes in it much good.﴾ That is: do not separate from them merely because of the soul's aversion, for it may dislike what is more upright in religion and greater in good, and it may love what is the opposite. Let your consideration be toward what is more beneficial for religion and closer to good. ʿAsā (perhaps) originally signifies cause (ʿillah), so it was placed in its stead. The meaning is: if you dislike them, then be patient with them, for perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you.

﴿And if you desire to exchange one spouse for another﴾: that is, to divorce one wife and marry another. ﴿and you have given one of them﴾: that is, one of the wives. The pronoun is plural because by "spouse" he means the category (the species). ﴿a great amount﴾: a large quantity of wealth. ﴿then do not take anything from it﴾: that is, from the great amount. ﴿Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial and reproach, meaning: would you take it while being slanderers and sinners? It may also be read in the accusative as an expression of cause (al-ʻilla), as in your saying, "I sat out of the battle out of cowardice," because taking it is caused by their slander and their committing of sins. It was said that a man among them, when he wished to marry a new woman, would accuse the wife he had of an indecency, so that she would be compelled to seek release from him by returning what he had given her, so that he could turn to marrying the new one. Therefore they were forbidden from this. Al-buhtan (slander) is a lie by which the one it is told against is taken aback, and it may also be used for a false action; for this reason it is interpreted here as wrongdoing (al-zulm).

﴿And how could you take it when you have gone in to one another﴾: a denial of reclaiming the bridal gift (mahr), while the state is that he has reached her through physical intimacy, has entered upon her, and the mahr has become firmly due. ﴿And they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾: a firm pledge, which is the right of companionship and intimacy, or what Allah has bound them with regarding their wives by His saying: ﴿either to retain them in kindness or to release them in good manner﴾, or what the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to with his saying: «You have taken them under the trust of Allah, and you have made lawful their private parts by the word of Allah.»(p-67)

﴿And if you desire to exchange one spouse for another﴾: that is, to divorce one wife and marry another. ﴿and you have given one of them﴾: that is, one of the wives. The pronoun is plural because by "spouse" he means the category (the species). ﴿a great amount﴾: a large quantity of wealth. ﴿then do not take anything from it﴾: that is, from the great amount. ﴿Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial and reproach, meaning: would you take it while being slanderers and sinners? It may also be read in the accusative as an expression of cause (al-ʻilla), as in your saying, "I sat out of the battle out of cowardice," because taking it is caused by their slander and their committing of sins. It was said that a man among them, when he wished to marry a new woman, would accuse the wife he had of an indecency, so that she would be compelled to seek release from him by returning what he had given her, so that he could turn to marrying the new one. Therefore they were forbidden from this. Al-buhtan (slander) is a lie by which the one it is told against is taken aback, and it may also be used for a false action; for this reason it is interpreted here as wrongdoing (al-zulm).

﴿And how could you take it when you have gone in to one another﴾: a denial of reclaiming the bridal gift (mahr), while the state is that he has reached her through physical intimacy, has entered upon her, and the mahr has become firmly due. ﴿And they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾: a firm pledge, which is the right of companionship and intimacy, or what Allah has bound them with regarding their wives by His saying: ﴿either to retain them in kindness or to release them in good manner﴾, or what the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to with his saying: «You have taken them under the trust of Allah, and you have made lawful their private parts by the word of Allah.»(p-67)

﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married﴾: that is, do not marry the women whom your fathers married. He used "mā" rather than "man" because what is intended is the attribute (ṣifah). It has also been said that "mā" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah, a "mā" that turns the following clause into a verbal noun) with the sense of the object of the verbal noun. ﴿of women﴾ explains "what" under both readings. ﴿Except what has already passed﴾ is an exception from the meaning necessarily implied by the prohibition, as if it were said: "You will deserve punishment for marrying what your fathers married, except what has already passed." Or the exception is from the wording itself, for emphasis on the prohibition and its generality, as in the line of poetry:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords, with them, are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

The meaning is: "Do not marry the wives of your fathers, except what has already passed, if it is possible for you to marry them." It has also been said that the exception is disconnected (munqaṭi', an exception not of the same category as what precedes it), and its meaning is: "But what has already passed," for there is no blame for it, since it has been settled. ﴿Indeed it was an abomination and hateful﴾: this is the reason (ʿillah) for the prohibition, meaning: their marriage was an abomination in the sight of God, which He did not permit for any nation among the nations, and it was detested (mamqūtan) in the sight of people of honour (dhawī al-murūʾāt). For this reason the son of a man born of his father's wife was called "al-maqtī" (the hated one). ﴿And evil is the way﴾: it is the way of one who sees it and does it.

Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, the daughters of your brother, and the daughters of your sister. It is not meant to forbid their persons, but to forbid marrying them, because that is the most important of what is intended from them, and because it is what is immediately understood, like the prohibition of eating in His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾. Also, what comes before it and after it concerns marriage. "Your mothers" includes whoever bore you, or bore someone who bore you, however far up. "Your daughters" includes whomever you bore, or who bore someone you bore, however far down. "Your sisters" means sisters in all three ways (full, paternal, and maternal). The same applies to the rest. The paternal aunt is every female whose offspring is a male who fathered you. The maternal aunt is every female whose offspring is a female who bore you, near or far. "The daughters of your brother and the daughters of your sister" includes both near and far descendants.

﴿And your mothers who suckled you, and your sisters through fosterage﴾. God made fosterage equivalent to lineage, to the point that He called the nursing woman a mother and the nursed child a sister. Its rulings follow the analogy of lineage, with regard to the nursing woman and the father of the child whose milk she produced.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by fosterage."

The exception of a man's son's sister and his brother's mother through fosterage from this general principle is not correct, for their prohibition arises from affinity (musaharah), not from lineage.

﴿And your wives' mothers, and your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage﴾. He first mentioned the prohibitions of lineage, then the prohibitions of fosterage, because it has a bond like the bond of lineage, and then the prohibitions of affinity, because their prohibition is incidental to the interest of marriage. "Rabā'ib" is the plural of "rabība." The "rabīb" is a woman's child by another man, named so because he is typically raised as one raises one's own child. It is on the pattern of "faʿīl" in the sense of "mafʿūl," and the feminine "tā'" was attached because it became a noun. "Min nisā'ikum" is connected to "rabā'ibukum." The relative clause "allātī" with its complement is an attribute of it, qualifying the wording, and the ruling by consensus (ijmāʿ, agreement of scholars) is a consequence of the structure. It is not permissible to connect it to "the mothers" as well, because if you connect it to the stepdaughters, "min" is initial (ibtidāʾiyya, indicating origin), whereas if you connect it to the mothers, that is not permitted, but it must be an explanation of "nisā'ikum." According to the majority of the literati, a single word is not carried to two meanings, except if you make it for connection, as in his saying:

"When you attempt wickedness against a lion,
then I am not of yours, and you are not of mine."

The meaning is that the mothers of women and their daughters are connected to them. But the Messenger (ﷺ) distinguished between them, saying about a man who married a woman and divorced her before consummating the marriage: "There is no harm in his marrying her daughter, but it is not lawful for him to marry her mother."

Most scholars went to this view, except that it is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he restricted the prohibition in both cases. It is not permissible for the second relative clause to be an attribute of the two women, because their governing word differs. The purpose of his saying "under your guardianship" is to strengthen and complete the cause. The meaning is that when you have consummated marriage with the stepdaughters' mothers, and they are in your care or about to be, the resemblance between them and your children grows stronger, and they become worthy of being treated as your children. It is not a restriction of the prohibition, and to this view went the majority of scholars.

It is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he made it a condition. The "mothers" and the "stepdaughters" both cover near and far. His saying "with whom you have consummated" means you had intercourse with them behind the veil. It is a kināya (euphemism) for intercourse. What is not fornication still affects the prohibition of affinity, such as intercourse by mistaken doubt (shubha), or by ownership of the right hand. According to Abu Hanifa, touching the married woman and the like is equivalent to consummation.

﴿If you have not consummated with them, there is no blame upon you﴾. This is an explicit statement after an implication, to block analogy (qiyās).

﴿And the wives of your sons﴾: their wives. The wife was called "ḥalīla" because she is lawful (ḥilla) to him, or because she dwells (ḥulūl) with the husband. ﴿Who are from your loins﴾: this excludes adopted sons, and does not exclude sons' sons. ﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾: this is in the nominative position, conjoined to the prohibited persons. Apparently the prohibition is not confined to marriage, for just as the enumerated persons are prohibited in marriage, they are prohibited in ownership by the right hand. For this reason, Uthman and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "One verse forbade them, and one verse made them lawful," meaning this verse.

As for His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, preferred the prohibition, while Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, preferred permission. Ali's view is more evident, because the verse of permission is specified for other than this case, and because of the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "Lawful and unlawful never gather except that the unlawful prevails."

﴿Except what has already passed﴾. This is either an exception from a necessary implication, or a disconnected exception whose meaning is: "but what has already passed is forgiven," because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 24:

﴿And the married women among women﴾: those who have husbands. They are made chaste (muhsanat) either by marriage or by their husbands. Al-Kisa'i read the vowel of the ṣād (i.e. al-muḥṣināt, with a kasra) throughout the Qur'an, because they have guarded their chastity (furuj). ﴿Except what your right hands possess﴾: he means those among them who were taken captive while they had disbelieving husbands; they are lawful to their captors. Marriage is annulled by capture, according to the saying of Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him: "We took captives on the day of Awtas, and they had disbelieving husbands. We disliked to have intercourse with them, so we asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and the verse was revealed, and we made them lawful to us." It was this that al-Farazdaq meant by his verse:

؎ And a woman with a husband, whom our spears have made wed [to us], is lawful to whoever consummates with her, she not having been divorced.

Abu Hanifa said: if a married couple is taken captive, the marriage is not annulled and she is not lawful to the captor. The unrestricted wording of the verse and the hadith is a proof against him. ﴿The decree of Allah upon you﴾: a verbal noun for emphasis, meaning Allah has prescribed upon you the prohibition of these women as a decree (kitaban). It was also read as "kutub" Allah, in the plural and nominative, meaning: these are the obligations of Allah upon you; and "wa-kataba Allah" with the verbal form. ﴿And lawful to you﴾: it is conjoined to the implied verb that governs "the decree of Allah." Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read it in the passive voice, conjoined to "have been made unlawful" (hurrimat). ﴿Beyond that﴾: other than the eight prohibited categories mentioned. Through the Sunnah there is excluded from this general permission what has the same meaning as those mentioned, such as all the prohibitions by fosterage, and the combining of a woman with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt. ﴿That you seek [them] with your wealth, as chaste ones, not as fornicators﴾: an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). The meaning: it is made lawful for you, beyond that, for the purpose of your seeking women with your wealth by paying their bridal gifts (mahr) or their prices, while you are chaste and not fornicators. It is also permissible that the object of "seek" is not stated, as if it were said: for the purpose of their spending your wealth, being chaste and not fornicators; or it is a substitute (badal al-ishtimal) for "beyond that." The Hanafis used this verse to argue that the bridal gift must necessarily be property; but there is no proof in it. Ihsan is chastity, for it is a fortification of the self against blame and punishment; and sifah is fornication, from safh, which is the pouring of semen, for that is its aim. ﴿So for whatever you have enjoyed from them﴾: whoever you have enjoyed from among the women you married, or "so for whatever you have sought from them" of intercourse or contract with them. ﴿Then give them their wages﴾: their bridal gifts, for the bridal gift is in exchange for enjoyment. ﴿As an obligation﴾: a circumstantial phrase (hal) from "wages," meaning obligatory; or an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning a gift that is obligatory; or a verbal noun for emphasis. ﴿And there is no blame upon you in what you mutually agree upon after the obligation﴾: in what is added to the stated amount or reduced from it by mutual consent, or in what they both agree upon regarding maintenance, residence, or separation. It has been said: the verse was revealed concerning temporary marriage (mut'ah), which was for three days when Mecca was conquered, and was then abrogated (naskh), for it is narrated that he (ﷺ) permitted it, then in the morning he said: "O people, I had commanded you to enjoy these women; indeed Allah has prohibited that until the Day of Resurrection."

It is the marriage fixed for a known term; it is so named because its purpose is merely the enjoyment of the woman, or her being provided for with what is given. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, permitted it, then retracted. ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of the interests, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He has legislated of rulings.

﴿And whoever among you cannot afford﴾ means cannot afford wealth and means, and the root of *tawl* is surplus and abundance. ﴿to marry free believing women﴾ is in the accusative position as the object of *tawl*. Alternatively, it is a qualifier of an implied verb: "whoever among you cannot attain (*yaʿtaliya*) marrying free women," or "whoever among you lacks wealth sufficient to reach marrying free women, meaning the free women (*al-ḥarāʾir*)," as indicated by His words: ﴿from those whom your right hands possess of your believing slave girls﴾, meaning believing slave women (*al-imāʾ*). The apparent sense of the verse is a proof for al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that marrying a slave woman is forbidden to one who possesses what would serve as the dower of a free woman, and that marrying a Scripturist (*kitābiyya*) slave woman is forbidden absolutely. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, interpreted *ṭawl* of free women as owning their beds (i.e., being able to provide for them), on the basis that marriage (*nikāḥ*) means sexual intercourse (*waṭʾ*), and he construed His words ﴿of your believing slave girls﴾ as referring to what is preferable. He also construed it this way in His words: "the believing free women." Some of our companions (the Shafiʿis) construed it as a restriction as well, and permitted marrying a slave woman for one who is able to marry a free Scripturist woman but not a believing one, out of caution against mixing with unbelievers and befriending them. What is feared in marrying a slave woman is the enslavement of the child and the humiliation it entails and the diminution of the husband's right. ﴿And Allah knows best your faith﴾: so they are content with the outward appearance of faith, for He is the one who knows the inner secrets. Faith varies among you, for a slave woman may surpass a free woman in it. It is your duty to regard the excellence of faith and not the excellence of lineage. The intent is to make them comfortable with marrying slave women and to prevent them from disdaining it, and this supports that. ﴿You are of one another﴾: you and your slaves are related, your lineage going back to Adam and your religion being Islam. ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾, meaning their owners. Requiring their permission is absolute and carries no implication otherwise. Moreover, they may conduct the contract themselves, so that the Hanafis may argue from it. ﴿And give them their wages﴾, meaning pay their dowers (*mahr*) to them with the permission of their people. The object is omitted because it was mentioned earlier. Or, it means to their masters (*mawālīhinna*), and the word "masters" is omitted, since it is known that the dower belongs to the master because it is the compensation for his right, so it must be paid to him. Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the dower belongs to the slave woman, following the apparent sense, "in accordance with what is customary, without delay, harm, or diminution." ﴿Chaste (*muḥṣanāt*)﴾ means modest. ﴿Not fornicating (*musāfiḥāt*)﴾ means not openly practicing fornication (*sifāḥ*). ﴿Nor taking secret lovers (*akhdān*)﴾ means private friends. ﴿And when they are married (*uḥṣinna*)﴾ through marriage. Abu Bakr and Hamza read it with an opening *hamza* and *ṣād* (*ufiʾna*... as *uḥṣinna* with *fatḥa*), while the rest read it with a *ḍamma* on the *hamza* and a *kasra* on the *ṣād*. ﴿But if they commit a lewd act (*fāḥisha*) of fornication, then upon them is half of the punishment (*ʿadhāb*) of the chaste women, meaning the free women,﴾ namely the prescribed punishment (*ḥadd*), in accordance with His words: ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾. This indicates that the *ḥadd* of a slave is half the *ḥadd* of a free person, and that they are not stoned, because stoning cannot be halved. ﴿That﴾, meaning marrying slave women, is ﴿for one among you who fears falling into sin (*ʿanat*)﴾, meaning who fears falling into fornication. *ʿAnat* in its original sense is the breaking of a bone after it has been set, and it is used figuratively for any hardship and harm, and there is no greater harm than committing sin through the most vile abominations. It has been said that what is meant is the *ḥadd*, and that this is another condition for marrying slave women. ﴿And that you be patient is better for you﴾, meaning your restraint from marrying slave women, while remaining chaste, is better for you. He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Free women are the goodness of the house, and slave women are its ruin." ﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾ toward one who does not endure patiently. ﴿Merciful﴾ in that He has granted him a concession.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 26:

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ what He has made you worship through the lawful (ḥalāl) and the unlawful (ḥarām), or what is hidden from you of your welfare (maṣāliḥ) and the excellence of your deeds. The object of "yurīdu" is "liyubayyina," and the lam (lām) has been added to emphasize the sense of futurity (al-istiqbāl) necessarily implied by the act of desiring, as in the verse of Qays ibn Sa'd:

I desired, so that people would know that
the trousers of Qays, and the delegations as witnesses...

It is also said that the object is omitted, and that "liyubayyina" is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), meaning: He desires the truth for its sake. ﴿And guide you to the ways (sunan) of those before you﴾: the methods (manāhij) of those who preceded you from among the people of rectitude, so that you may follow their paths. ﴿And turn to you in forgiveness﴾: and forgive your sins; or He guides you to what will restrain you from acts of disobedience and urges you to repentance; or to what will serve as expiation (kaffārah) for your misdeeds. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of them ﴿All-Wise﴾ in their placement.

**[Al-Baydawi, *Anwar al-Tanzil*, on Surah an-Nisa' 4:27–28]**

﴿And Allah desires to turn to you [in forgiveness]﴾. He repeated it for emphasis and intensification. ﴿But those who follow their desires desire that you deviate [from the truth] with a great deviation﴾. He means the wicked (*fajarah*), for following desires means being driven by them. As for the one who indulges in what the Law (*shar'*) has permitted of them, and nothing else, he in reality follows the Law, not his desires.

It is also said: they are the Magians (*Majus*, Zoroastrians). It is also said: they are the Jews, for they permit marriage to a half-sister from the father's side, to a brother's daughter, and to a sister's daughter. ﴿That you deviate﴾ from the truth by agreeing with them in following desires and permitting what is forbidden. ﴿A great deviation﴾, compared with the deviation of one who commits a sin occasionally without considering it permissible.

﴿Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you﴾. For this reason He prescribed for you the *shir'ah* (sacred law) of the *hanifiyyah* (the upright, original monotheistic way), which is tolerant, easy and simple, and He granted you concessions in difficult circumstances, such as the permission to marry a slave woman. ﴿And man was created weak﴾, unable to restrain himself from desires and unable to bear the hardships of acts of obedience.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "There are eight verses in Surat an-Nisa' which are better for this community than everything the sun rises upon and sets over. These three are: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾, ﴿Allah does not forgive that He be associated with]﴾, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] by an atom's weight; and whoever does an evil will be recompensed for it﴾, and ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾"
