Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 74:

﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter.﴾ That is, those who sell it in exchange for it. The meaning is: if these people hold back from fighting, then let fight the sincere ones who spend themselves seeking the Hereafter. Or [the meaning is]: those who buy it and prefer it over the Hereafter, namely the laggards. The meaning is an exhortation to them to abandon what was related about them. ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or achieves victory, We shall bestow upon him a great reward.﴾ He promised him a great reward whether he was victorious or was defeated, as an encouragement to fight and as a refutation of their saying: "Allah has blessed me, for I was not present with them as a witness." He said "is killed or achieves victory" only as a reminder that the striver should stand firm in the battle until he honors himself with martyrdom or with victory and triumph for the religion, and that his intention should not be directly the killing, but rather the elevation of the truth and the strengthening of the religion.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 75:**

﴿Why should you not fight in the way of God﴾: "وَما لَكُمْ" is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). "لا تُقاتِلُونَ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ" is a circumstantial clause (hal), and its governing element (al-'amil) is what the adverbial phrase contains of the meaning of a verb.

﴿And of the oppressed﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the name of God, Exalted is He, meaning "and in the way of the oppressed," which is their rescue from captivity and the protection of them from the enemy. Or it is conjoined to "sabil" with an elided genitive (al-mudaf al-mahdhuf), meaning "and in the liberation of the oppressed." It is also permissible to read it in the accusative as a specification (al-ikhtisas), for the way of God, Exalted is He, encompasses all doors of good, and the liberation of the weak among the Muslims from the hands of the disbelievers is the greatest and most specific of them. ﴿Of the men and the women and the children﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of "the oppressed," and they are the Muslims who remained in Mecca, being prevented by the polytheists, or who were too weak to emigrate, humiliated and tested. The mention of "the children" is for emphasis in urging, and as an alert to the extreme of the polytheists' oppression, to the point that their harm reached even the young children, and that their supplication was answered because of their participation in the prayer, so that they would share in drawing down mercy and warding off calamity.

It has been said that what is meant by it is the slaves, male and female, and it is the plural of "walid." ﴿Who say: Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are wrongdoers, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper﴾. God answered their supplication by making it easy for some of them to go out to Medina, and He made for those who remained among them the best protector and helper through the conquest of Mecca over His Prophet ﷺ. So He took charge of them and helped them, then He appointed over them 'Attab ibn Usayd, who protected them and aided them until they became the most honoured people of it. "The town" is Mecca, and "wrongdoers" is its attribute. Its masculine form is for the masculinity of what is attributed to it, for when an active or passive participle applies to other than the one it belongs to, it behaves like a verb, which is masculinized or feminized according to what governs it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 76:

﴿Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah﴾, [fighting] by which they reach Allah, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿And those who disbelieve fight in the cause of al-Taghut﴾ [fighting] which leads them to Satan. ﴿So fight the allies of Satan﴾. Since He had mentioned the aim of the two groups, He commanded His allies to fight the allies of Satan. Then He encouraged them with His words: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾, meaning: his plot against the believers, in comparison with (p-85) the plot of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, against the disbelievers, is weak and of no account. So do not fear his allies, for their reliance is on the weakest and feeblest of things.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 77:

﴿Have you not seen those to whom it was said, "Restrain your hands"﴾ i.e., from fighting. ﴿"And establish the prayer and give the zakat"﴾ and occupy yourselves with what you have been commanded.

﴿But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them feared men as they feared God﴾ they feared the unbelievers, that they would kill them, as they feared God that He would send down His punishment upon them. The "idha" (behold, suddenly) here is the response (jawab) to "lamma" (when), and "fariqun" (a party) is the subject (mubtada'), of which "minhum" (of them) is the qualifier (sifah), and "yakhshawna" (they fear) is the predicate (khabar). "Ka-khashyati Allah" (as they feared God) is an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, and it stands in the position of a verbal noun (masdar) or of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yakhshawna," with the meaning: they fear men with a fear like the fear of God held by those who fear Him.

﴿Or even more intensely﴾ this is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon it if you make it a circumstantial clause; but if you make it a verbal noun, then it is not. This is because the elative (af'al al-tafdil), when it governs what follows it in the accusative, is not of the same kind as what precedes it; rather, it is coordinated upon the name of God Most High. That is: "and as the fear of God Most High, or as a fear more intense than His," supposing it, except that you make "khashyah" (fear) possess a fear, as in their saying "jiddu jiddihi" (the utmost of his effort), with the meaning: they fear men with a fear like the fear of God Most High, or with a fear more intense than the fear of God.

﴿And they say, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term."﴾ This is a request for an extension of the period of restraint from fighting, out of fear of death. It is possible that they did not utter it with their tongues, but rather said it within themselves, and God Most High related it about them.

﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little"﴾ swift to pass away. ﴿"And the Hereafter is better for one who fears God, and you will not be wronged a fraction (fatil)."﴾ That is: you will not be diminished the least thing of your reward, so do not turn away from it, or from your appointed terms.

And Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-la yuzlamun" (they will not be wronged) with the third person, because of the prior mention of the third person (ghaybah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 78:

﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾. It has been read in the nominative (ara:fa'), by omitting the fa' (the particle of consequence), as in His words: "Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them." Or it is taken as an independent sentence (kalam mubtada'), and "wherever" (aynama) is connected to "you will not be wronged" (la tuzlamun).

﴿And even if you were in towers built up high﴾: in lofty palaces or fortresses. The word burooj (towers) originally means houses on the outskirts of palaces, from tabarrajat al-mar'ah (the woman displayed herself) when she showed herself. It has also been read mashidah with a kasra on the ya', as a description of it using the description of its builder, as in their saying qasidah sha'irah (a poem that composes itself). Mashidah is from shada al-qasr (he built up the palace) when he raised it.

﴿And if a good thing befalls them, they say, "This is from Allah"; and if an evil thing befalls them, they say, "This is from you."﴾ Just as good (hasanah) and evil (sayyi'ah) are used for obedience and disobedience, they are also used for blessing and affliction, and these are what is meant in the verse. That is: if a blessing befalls them, such as fertility, they attribute it to Allah, glorified and exalted be He; and if an affliction befalls them, such as drought, they attribute it to you (the Prophet) and say, "This is only because of your ill omen," just as the Jews said: "Since Muhammad entered Medina, its fruits have decreased and its prices have risen."

﴿Say, "All is from Allah."﴾ That is, He extends and restricts as He wills.

﴿So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any speech?﴾ That is, a discourse by which they could be admonished, namely the Qur'an; for if they understood it and reflected on its meanings, they would know that all is from Allah, glorified and exalted be He. Or "speech" (hadith) means any utterance, like that of beasts that have no understanding, or an event arising from the vicissitudes of time, so that they would reflect on it and know that the One who withholds and extends is Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

(p-86) ﴿What befalls you﴾, O human, ﴿of good﴾, i.e. of blessing, ﴿is from Allah﴾, meaning by His bounty, for every act of obedience a person performs does not repay the blessing of existence, so how could it necessitate anything else? For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "No one enters Paradise except by the mercy of Allah, the Exalted." It was said: "Not even you?" He said: "Not even I."

﴿And what befalls you of evil﴾, i.e. of affliction, ﴿is from yourself﴾, because it is the self that is the cause of it, by inviting it through acts of disobedience. This does not contradict His words, glorified and exalted be He: "Say: all is from Allah." For all is from Him in terms of creating and bringing about, but good is a favour and a bestowal, while evil is a recompense and retribution, as 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "No Muslim is afflicted with fatigue or hardship, not even a thorn that pricks him or the loosening of the strap of his sandal, except that it is because of a sin, and Allah pardons more than that." As you see, these two verses offer no proof either for us or for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that holds human acts are created by the servant).

﴿And We have sent you to the people as a messenger﴾: this is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), used for emphasis if the prepositional phrase is attached to the verb, and for generality if it is attached to the word "messenger", meaning a messenger to all the people, as in His words, exalted be He: "And We have not sent you except to all mankind." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun), as in the line: "nor a lying speech coming out of my mouth."

﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾ to your message, by establishing the miracles.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 80–81:

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, is in reality only a conveyer (of the message), while the one who commands is Allah, glorified and exalted.

It is narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever loves me has loved Allah, and whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah." The hypocrites said: "He has committed shirk while he forbids it; he only wants us to take him as a lord, just as the Christians took Jesus as a lord." So this was revealed.

﴿And whoever turns away﴾ from his obedience. ﴿We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾, watching over their deeds and calling them to account for them. Your duty is only to convey (the message), and upon Us is the reckoning. The phrase is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the kāf (the "you" in "sent you").

﴿And they say﴾ when you command them with a matter: ﴿"Obedience"﴾, i.e., our affair is obedience, or obedience is from us. Its original form is the accusative (naṣb) as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its nominative (rafʿ) form is used to indicate permanence. ﴿Then when they go out from your presence﴾, i.e., depart. ﴿A group of them plots at night other than what you say﴾, i.e., they devise something contrary to what you told them, or contrary to the acceptance and guarantee of obedience that they had given you. The verb bayyata (to plot at night) may derive either from bayta (spending the night), because affairs are arranged at night, or from bayt al-shiʿr (a verse-line) or the built house, because it arranges and organizes (matters). Abu ʿAmr and Hamza read "bayyata ṭāʾifatun" with idghām (assimilation), because the two letters are close in their point of articulation. ﴿And Allah records what they plot at night﴾, recording it in their scrolls for requital, or within what is revealed to you so that you may be acquainted with their secrets. ﴿So turn away from them﴾, pay little heed to them, or keep aloof from them. ﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾ in all matters, especially in their affair. ﴿And Allah suffices as a Guardian﴾, He will suffice you against their harm and will avenge you on them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 80–81:

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, is in reality only a conveyer (of the message), while the one who commands is Allah, glorified and exalted.

It is narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever loves me has loved Allah, and whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah." Why do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? ﴿Afalā yatadabbarūna al-Qur'ān﴾ — they contemplate its meanings and look closely into what it contains. The root of tadabbur (reflection) is looking at the back-ends (adbār) of a thing.

﴿Wa-law kāna min ʿindi ghayri Allāh﴾ — that is: even if it were from the speech of human beings, as the disbelievers claim.

﴿La-wajadū fīhi ikhtilāfan kathīran﴾ — [they would have found in it much discrepancy], in the form of contradiction of meaning and variation of composition, some of it being eloquent and some of it weak, some of it being difficult to match and some of it easy; the correspondence of some of its reports about the future with what actually happened but not others; and the agreement of reason with some of its rulings but not others. This is what induction indicates, due to the deficiency of human capacity. Perhaps its mention here is to draw attention to the fact that the difference among the rulings previously mentioned is not due to contradiction in the ruling, but rather to the differing circumstances, rulings and interests.

(p-87) ﴿And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear﴾ — something that calls for security or for fear. ﴿they spread it abroad﴾ — they disclose it, as some of the weaker Muslims used to do when news reached them of the expeditions (sarāyā) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or when the Messenger (ﷺ) informed them of what had been revealed to him, such as a promise of victory, or a warning of threat from the disbelievers; they would spread it abroad, owing to their lack of firmness, and so their spreading it was corrupting. The bā' (in "bihi") is either superfluous, or the verb idhā'a is taken to imply the meaning of "speaking about". ﴿And if they had referred it﴾ — i.e., if they had referred that news ﴿to the Messenger and to those in authority among them﴾ — to his judgment and the judgment of the senior companions who were discerning in affairs, or to the commanders. ﴿They would have known it﴾ — they would have known what they were told, in what manner it should be mentioned. ﴿Those among them who investigate it﴾ — who extract its courses of action through their experience and reflection. It was also said: they used to hear the rumours of the hypocrites and spread them, so that they would turn into calamity upon the Muslims. "And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them" — until they heard it from them and knew whether it should be spread; for the knowledge of this would come from those who investigate it from the Messenger and those in authority; i.e., they extract its knowledge from them. The root of istinbāṭ (extraction) is the extraction of nabaṭ, which is water that emerges from a well when it is first dug. ﴿And had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ — through the sending of the Messenger and the sending down of the Book. ﴿You would have followed Satan﴾ — and disbelief and error. ﴿except for a few﴾ — i.e., except for a few of you, upon whom Allah bestowed a superior intellect by which he was guided to the truth and rightness, and whom He protected from following Satan, such as Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl and Waraqah ibn Nawfal. Or: except for a little following, occurring rarely.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 84:

﴿So fight in the way of Allah﴾ — that is, [fight] even though they hold back and leave you alone. ﴿You are not burdened except with yourself﴾ — that is, you are only responsible for your own action; their opposition and their staying behind do not harm you. So advance to jihad, and even if no one helps you, indeed Allah is your Helper, not the armies.

It is narrated: "He (peace be upon him) invited the people to set out to Badr al-Sughra, but some of them disliked it, so this verse was revealed. He (peace be upon him) then set out with only seventy men, and he did not turn back for anyone."

It is also read as ﴿lā tukallaf﴾ with a jazm (the verb ending in a sukun), and as ﴿lā nukallif﴾ with a nun, in the active voice (bināʾ al-fāʿil), meaning: "We do not burden you except with your own action," not that "We do not burden anyone except yourself," in accordance with His saying: ﴿And urge the believers﴾ to fighting, since your only responsibility regarding them is exhortation. ﴿It may be that Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve﴾ — meaning the Quraysh — and He did so by casting terror into their hearts until they turned back. ﴿And Allah is stronger in might﴾ than the Quraysh. ﴿And stronger in punishment﴾ — that is, in torment — than them. This is a rebuke and a threat to those who did not follow him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 85:

﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession﴾ by which he observes the right of a Muslim and thereby repels harm from him or brings him benefit, seeking the Face of Allah, the Exalted. Among it is supplication for a Muslim. The Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "Whoever supplicates for his Muslim brother in his absence, it is answered for him, and the angel says to him: 'And for you is the like of that.'"

﴿He will have a share of it﴾, which is the reward of intercession and of being the cause of the good that results from it. ﴿And whoever intercedes with an evil intercession﴾ intending by it something forbidden. ﴿He will have a portion of its burden﴾, a share of its sin equal to it in measure. ﴿And Allah is ever, over all things, Muqit﴾, Omnipotent, from aqata ʿala al-shay' (to have power over a thing) when one is able to do it. He said:

"And one who bears a grudge, I withheld the grudge from him,
And I was over his ill will a muqit (one with power over it)."

Or it means Watchful, Guardian. Its derivation is from al-qut (sustenance), for it strengthens the body and preserves it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 86:

﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with one better than it, or return it.﴾ The majority (al-jumhur) hold that this refers to the salam (greeting of peace). It indicates that replying is obligatory, either with something better than it, which is to add to it, "and the mercy of God" (wa-rahmatu Allah); so if the Muslim says it, he adds "and His blessings" (wa-barakatuh), which is the utmost limit. Or [one replies] with its equivalent, (p-88) in accordance with what has been narrated: "A man said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: 'Peace be upon you.' He said: 'And upon you be peace and the mercy of God.' Another said: 'Peace be upon you and the mercy of God,' and he said: 'And upon you be peace and the mercy of God and His blessings.' Another said: 'Peace be upon you and the mercy of God and His blessings,' and he said: 'And upon you.' The man said: 'You have left us short, so where is what God Most High said?' and he recited the verse. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'You did not leave any excess for me, so I returned to you its equivalent.'"

That is because it comprehensively includes the aspects of what is sought: safety from harms, the attainment of benefits, and their permanence; and from this it was said [that the wording is comprehensive]. Or the "or" (aw) is for giving a choice between a Muslim greeting another with part of the greeting and greeting with its full form. This obligation is a collective obligation (fard kifayah). Wherever greeting is legislated, it is not to be offered during the khutbah (sermon), the recitation of the Qur'an, in the bathhouse, while relieving oneself, or the like. The word tahiyyah (greeting) is originally a verbal noun of "hayyaka Allah" (may God grant you life), used for the informative sense of life; then it was used for the pronouncement and supplication with that; then it was applied to every supplication, and it came to be predominantly used for the salam. It was also said that the intended meaning of tahiyyah is a gift, and the obligation of reciprocating it, or returning it to the one who gave the gift; and this is an old opinion of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him. ﴿Indeed, God is ever Reckoner over all things﴾ He will call you to account for the greeting and other things.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 87:

﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him.﴾ It is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), or Allah is the mubtada' and the khabar is ﴿He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾, i.e., Allah, and Allah will surely resurrect you from your graves to the Day of Resurrection. Or it is "reaching it" (mufdina ilayhi), or "on the Day of Resurrection." And ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). The qiyam and the qiyamah are like the tilab and the tilabah, and it is the standing of people from the graves or for the reckoning. ﴿There is no doubt about it﴾: "in the Day" or "in the gathering," so it is a hal (circumstantial clause) from the Day, or a sifah (qualifier) for the verbal noun. ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ It is a denial that anyone could be more truthful than Him, for falsehood cannot find its way into His report in any respect, because that would be a deficiency, and deficiency is impossible for Allah.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 88:

﴿So what is [the matter] with you concerning the hypocrites?﴾ That is: why have you become divided over the matter of the hypocrites? ﴿Two groups﴾: that is, two factions, and you did not agree upon their disbelief. The reason is that some of them asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to go out to the desert because of the unsuitability of Medina (ijtiwa’ al-madina). When they went out, they kept riding (rahlayn), stage by stage (marhalatan marhalatan), until they joined the polytheists, so the Muslims differed concerning their Islam. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning those who stayed behind on the day of Uhud, or concerning a people who emigrated and then returned, pretexting the unsuitability of Medina and longing for their homeland, or concerning a people who displayed Islam and held back from emigration. ﴿Two groups﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) whose governing element is "lakum," like your saying: "What is the matter with you, standing?" ﴿Concerning the hypocrites﴾ is a circumstantial clause from "two groups," meaning dividing into two factions regarding them; or it is from the pronoun, meaning: why do you divide concerning them? The meaning of division is derived from "two groups." ﴿And God has overturned them for what they earned﴾: He returned them to the ruling of the disbelievers, or He overturned them by making them fuel for the Fire. The root of raks is returning a thing upside down. ﴿Do you wish to guide those whom God has led astray?﴾ That is, that you would make them among the guided. ﴿And whomever God leads astray, you will not find for him a way﴾ to guidance.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 89:

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved﴾ They wish that you would disbelieve in the same way as their disbelief. ﴿So that you would be equal﴾ so that you would be equal with them in misguidance. This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "that you would disbelieve." Had it been put in the accusative (naṣb) as a response (jawab) to the wish (tamanni), it would have been permissible. ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾ So do not take them as friends until they believe and you verify their faith by an emigration that is for Allah and His Messenger, not for the aims of this world. "The way of Allah" is what He has commanded to be followed. ﴿But if they turn away﴾ from faith outwardly manifested by emigration, or from displaying faith. ﴿Then seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾ just as with the other disbelievers. ﴿And take not from among them a protector or a helper﴾ meaning, dissociate from them entirely, and do not accept from them any guardianship or support.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 90:

﴿Except those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾ This is an exception from His saying, "So take them and kill them," meaning: except those who connect themselves to and arrive at a people who have made a covenant with you, and who give up fighting against you. The people are Khuza'ah. It is also said: they are the Aslamiyyun, for when he (ﷺ) went out toward Makkah he made a truce with Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami, on the condition that he would not help him nor help anyone against him, and whoever sought refuge with him would have the same protection as his own. It is also said: they are Banu Bakr ibn Zayd Manat. ﴿Or those who come to you﴾ This is conjoined to the relative clause, meaning: or those who come to you, restraining from fighting you and fighting their own people. He excepted from those commanded to be seized and killed those who left the combatants and joined the covenanted ones, or who came to the Messenger (ﷺ) and refrained from fighting both parties. Or it is in the manner of describing a people, as if it were said: except those who join a people who are covenanted, or a people who restrain from fighting you and from fighting against you. The first is more apparent, due to His saying, "So if they withdraw from you." It was also read without the conjunction, on the basis that it is a description following a description, or an explanation of "yasiluna" (join), or a new sentence. ﴿Their hearts are constricted﴾ is a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied; what indicates this is that it was read as "hasrat sudurihim" and "hasarat sudurihim." Or it is an explanation of "jaa'ukum." It is also said that it is a description of an omitted noun, meaning: they came to you as a people whose hearts are constricted, and they are Banu Mudlij, who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) not fighting. Al-hasr means constriction and contraction. ﴿That they fight you or fight their people﴾ meaning: because they fight you, or because they fight their people, or out of dislike that they would fight you. ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you﴾ by strengthening their hearts, expanding their breasts, and removing terror from them. ﴿So they would have fought you﴾ and not refrained from you. ﴿So if they withdraw from you and do not fight you﴾ if they do not confront you. ﴿And offer you peace﴾ meaning submission and compliance. ﴿Then Allah has not made for you any way against them﴾ meaning He has not permitted you to seize or kill them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 91:

﴿You will find others who wish to be safe from you and to be safe from their own people.﴾ They are Asad and Ghatafan. It is also said they were the Banu Abd al-Dar, who came to Medina and displayed Islam so that they would be safe from the Muslims; but when they returned, they disbelieved. ﴿Every time they are returned to disorder⦆ they call to disbelief and to fighting the Muslims. ﴿They are plunged back into it﴾ they return to it and turn it over in the most vile way. ﴿So if they do not withdraw from you, nor offer you peace, nor restrain their hands﴾ means: nor cast the covenant back to you. ﴿Restrain their hands﴾ from fighting you. ﴿Then seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾ wherever you have power over them, for mere restraint of hand does not necessarily cancel the permission to engage them. ﴿And against them We have given you clear authority﴾ a manifest proof for confronting them with killing and taking captives, because of the obviousness of their enmity and the clarity of their disbelief and treachery; or, a manifest dominion, since We have permitted you to kill them.

(p-90) ﴿And it is not for a believer﴾ it is not proper for him, nor is it within his character, ﴿to kill a believer﴾ without right, ﴿except by mistake﴾. The phrase ﴿إلا خَطَأً﴾ (illā khaṭa'an, "except by mistake") is in the accusative. It is either a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) or an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). The meaning is: he does not kill him in any circumstance except the circumstance of error. Or: he does not kill him for any cause except error. Or it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "except a killing by mistake." It has also been said that ﴿ما كان﴾ (mā kāna, "it is not") is a negation carrying the sense of a prohibition, and that the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: but if he kills him by mistake, then his recompense is what is mentioned. Error (khaṭa') is that which is not accompanied by intention toward the act or the person, or that which is not intended to cause the taking of a soul in the usual way, or that which is not intended for a forbidden thing, such as shooting a Muslim among the ranks of the disbelievers while unaware that he is a Muslim, or it may be the act of one who is not legally responsible (ghayr al-mukallaf). It is recited as ﴿خطاءً﴾ with a long vowel, and as ﴿خطا﴾ on the pattern of ʿaṣā, with the hamza lightened. The verse was revealed concerning ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah, the maternal brother of Abū Jahl. He met Ḥārith ibn Zayd on a road, and Ḥārith had embraced Islam, but ʿAyyāsh did not know it, so he killed him.

﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then [there is] the freeing of a neck﴾, that is, upon him, or it is incumbent upon him, the freeing of a neck. Taḥrīr (freeing) means emancipation (iʿtāq). The free person is like the noble of a thing, as in the expression ḥurr al-wajh (free of face) for the most honorable place of it. It is so named because nobility belongs to free people and baseness to slaves. The word ﴿raqabah﴾ (neck) is used to express the person, just as the word "head" is used to express it. ﴿Believing﴾: it is judged that she is a Muslim, even if she is young. ﴿And a blood-money (diyah) delivered to his family﴾: it is to be paid to his heirs, who divide it as they divide the rest of the inheritance, based on the statement of Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Sufyān al-Kilābī: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to me instructing me to give the wife of Ashyam al-Ḍabābī an inheritance from the diyah of her husband."

It is borne by the ʿāqilah (the paternal kin who bear the diyah). If there are none, then it falls upon the public treasury (bayt al-māl). If there is none, then it is from his own property. ﴿Unless they forgo it﴾: that is, unless they give it up as charity to him (yataṣaddaqū). The pardoning of it is called ṣadaqah (charity), as an exhortation to it and an indication of its excellence. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every act of kindness is a charity."

The phrase ﴿وَهُوَ مُتَعَلِّقٌ بِعَلَيْهِ﴾ (wa huwa mutaʿallaq bi-ʿalayhi, "and it is connected to ʿalayhi") refers to the preceding ﴿عَلَيْهِ﴾ (ʿalayhi, "upon him"), or to ﴿مُسَلَّمَةٌ﴾ (musallamah, "delivered"). That is: the diyah is due from him, or he hands it over to his family, except in the case that they give it up to him as charity. Or the phrase is a temporal clause, in which case it stands in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the killer, or to the family, or it is an adverbial of time (ẓarf). ﴿If he was from a people hostile to you, and he was a believer, then [there is] the freeing of a believing neck﴾: that is, if the believing person who was killed was from a people of disbelieving combatants, or was among them and his faith was not known, then his killer owes the expiation (kaffārah) but not the diyah to his family, since there is no inheritance between him and them, and because they are combatants. ﴿And if he was from a people between you and them is a treaty, then a blood-money delivered to his family and the freeing of a believing neck﴾: that is, if he was from a people of disbelievers bound by treaty, or from the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah), then his ruling is the ruling of Muslims regarding the obligation of expiation and blood-money. Perhaps this applies when the one killed was a treaty-bound person, or when he had a Muslim heir. ﴿Then whoever does not find﴾ a neck, meaning he does not own one, nor has the means by which he could reach one.

﴿Then fasting for two consecutive months﴾: upon him, or it is obligatory upon him, the fasting of two consecutive months. ﴿As a repentance﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose: that is, this was prescribed as repentance, from "Allah accepted his repentance" when He accepted his repentance. Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun: "and Allah has accepted repentance from you." Or it is a circumstantial accusative with an omitted modifier: "upon him is fasting two months possessing repentance." ﴿From Allah﴾ is its qualifier. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of his state, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He commanded regarding his matter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 93:

﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever; and Allah has become angry with him, and has cursed him, and has prepared for him a great punishment.﴾ Because of the great threat it contains. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "The repentance of one who intentionally kills a believer is not accepted." Perhaps he intended it as a strong warning, since it is related from him that he held otherwise. The majority hold that it is specific to the one who does not repent, based on the words of Allah Most High: ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving to whoever repents﴾ and similar verses. In our view, it is either specific to the one who considers the killing lawful (istihlal), as mentioned by 'Ikrimah and others. This is supported by the fact that it was revealed concerning Maqis ibn Dababah, who found his brother Hisham slain among the Banu al-Najjar, and the slayer was not identified. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered them to pay him his blood-money, and they paid it to him. Then he attacked a Muslim and killed him, and returned to Makkah as an apostate. Or, the intended meaning of "abiding" (khulud) is a long stay, since the evidences are abundant that the sinful among the Muslims will not have their punishment last forever.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 94:

(p-91) ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth (idha darabtum) in the way of Allah﴾ — that is, when you travel and set out for the raid (ghazw). ﴿Then investigate (fa-tabayyanu)﴾ — seek clarity of the matter and its certainty, and do not hasten in it. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿fa-tathbutu﴾ in both places here, and in al-Hujurat, from ath-thabbut (verification, firm establishing). ﴿And do not say to one who offers you (alqa ilaykumu) peace (al-salam)﴾ — to one who greets you with the greeting of Islam. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read ﴿al-salama﴾ without the alif, meaning submission (al-istislam) and yielding (al-inqiyad), and al-salam has also been explained by this. ﴿You are not a believer﴾ — and I only did that seeking refuge (muta'awwidhan). It was also read as ﴿mu'ammanan﴾ with a fatha, meaning one to whom safety (aman) has been granted. ﴿Seeking the goods of this worldly life (ʿarad al-hayat al-dunya)﴾ — you seek its wealth, which is a quickly perishing trinket. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿taqulu﴾, indicating what drives them to haste and to abandoning verification. ﴿With Allah are abundant spoils (maghanim)﴾ for you ﴿kathirah﴾, which will make you independent of killing such a person for his property. ﴿Thus you were before﴾ — that is, when you first entered Islam, you uttered the two words of testimony, and thereby your blood and property were protected, without it being known whether your hearts agreed with your tongues. ﴿Then Allah conferred favour upon you﴾ — by becoming known for faith and steadfastness in the religion. ﴿Therefore investigate﴾ — and treat those who enter Islam as Allah treated you, and do not rush to kill them, assuming they entered it out of fear and dissimulation, for sparing a thousand unbelievers is less grave in the sight of Allah than killing one Muslim man. Its repetition is for emphasis on the gravity of the matter and for basing the ruling on the state of those described. ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ — Knowing of it and of its purpose, so do not be reckless in killing, and be cautious in it.

It is narrated: "The detachment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raided the people of Fadak, and they fled, but Mirdas remained, trusting in his Islam. When he saw the horses, he drove his sheep to a rocky ridge of the mountain and climbed up. When they caught up with him and shouted takbir, he too shouted takbir and descended, saying: 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon you.' Usamah killed him and seized his sheep." It has also been said that the verse was revealed concerning al-Miqdad, who passed by a man with a small flock and wanted to kill him, and the man said: "There is no god but Allah." He killed him anyway and said: "He wished he had fled with his family and property." In it is evidence for the validity of the faith of one who is coerced, and that the mujtahid may err, and that his error is forgiven.

The Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 95:

﴿Those who sit at home﴾ from the fighting. ﴿among the believers﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) qualifying "those who sit," or qualifying the pronoun within it. ﴿other than those with a harm﴾ is in the nominative as a qualifier (ṣifa) of "those who sit," because no specific people were intended by it, or it is a substitute (badal) for it. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī read it in the accusative, as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or an exception (istithnāʾ). It was also read in the genitive, as a qualifier of "the believers" or a substitute for them.

It is related from Zayd ibn Thābit that it was revealed while there was in it nothing except "other than those with a harm." Ibn Umm Maktūm said: "And how (can that be), when I am blind?" So the revelation overcame the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his assembly, and his thigh fell upon my thigh, until I feared that it would crush it. Then he was relieved of it and said: "Write: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm, and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their selves.﴾"

That is, there is no equality between them and those who sat back from jihad without an excuse. Its purpose is to remind of the difference between them, so that the one who sits back may desire jihad, seeking to raise his rank and out of disdain for the lowering of his station. ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their selves over those who sit back by a degree﴾ is a clause clarifying what the equality was negated in, and "those who sit back" is under the earlier restriction. "A degree" is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (nazʿ al-khāfid), meaning "by a degree," or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because it contains the meaning of preference and occupies the place of a single instance of it; or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "possessors of a degree." ﴿And to each﴾ of those who sit back and those who strive. ﴿Allah has promised the best﴾: the best reward, which is Paradise, because of the goodness of their creed and the sincerity of their intention. The difference lies only in the increase of deeds, which calls for greater reward. ﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit back with a great reward﴾: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because "favour" (faḍl) carries the meaning of "reward"; or it is the second object (mafʿūl thānī) of it, because it contains the meaning of "giving," as if it were said: "And He gave them an increase over (p-92) those who sit back, a great reward."

﴿Degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy﴾. Each of these is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for *ajran* (a reward). *Darajat* may also be in the accusative as a *masdar* (verbal noun, cognate accusative), as in your saying: "I struck him *aswatan*" (with lashes). *Ajran* may be in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) of *ha* (them), placed before it because it is indefinite (*nakira*). *Maghfiratan* and *rahmatan* are in the accusative as *masdar*, with a verb implied before them, i.e., *faʿalayhima* (He bestowed them upon them). He repeated the preference of the strivers and emphasised it both in summary (*ijmal*) and in detail (*tafsil*), to magnify jihad and to encourage it.

It has been said: the first (*darajat*) refers to what He granted them in this world of spoils, victory and good repute, and the second refers to what He made for them in the Hereafter. It has also been said: the first degree refers to the elevation of their rank with Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and the "degrees" refers to their dwellings in Paradise. It has been said that the first "those who sit" are those afflicted with harm (*al-aḍrāʾ*, i.e., the disabled), and the second "those who sit" are those whom He permitted to remain behind, being sufficed by others. It has also been said that the first "strivers" are those who fought the disbelievers, and the others are those who struggled against their own selves. In support of this is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad."

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾ of what may lapse from them. ﴿Merciful﴾ in what He has promised them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 97:

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾ may be read as past or present. It has also been read as «tawaffathum» and «tawaffāhum» in the present tense of (wafaytu, "to fulfil"), meaning that God fulfils (yuwaffī) the souls for the angels, so they (fa-yatawaffawnahā) take them in full, i.e., He enables them (yumakkinuhum) to take them fully, so they take them in full. ﴿wronging themselves﴾: in the state of their wronging themselves by abandoning emigration (al-hijrah) and agreeing with the disbelievers. It was revealed concerning people of Makkah who embraced Islam but did not emigrate when emigration was obligatory. ﴿They will say﴾: i.e., the angels, rebuking them. ﴿"In what were you?"﴾: in what matter of your religion were you?

﴿They will say, "We were oppressed in the land."﴾ They excuse themselves for what they were rebuked for by their weakness and inability to emigrate, or to manifest the religion and raise high the word of God. ﴿They will say﴾: i.e., the angels, denying them or rebuking them. ﴿"Was not the earth of God spacious so that you could have emigrated therein?"﴾ to another region, as the emigrants did to Madinah and Abyssinia. ﴿Their refuge is Hell﴾ because of their abandoning an obligation and their assisting the disbelievers. It is the predicate of inna, and the fa' in it is there because the noun contains the meaning of a conditional. "They said, 'In what were you?'" is a circumstantial clause from the angels, with qad implied, or the predicate is "they said," and the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., "they said to them." It is a clause conjoined to the preceding clause, derived from it.

﴿And evil is it as a destination﴾: their destination, or Hell. The verse is evidence for the obligation of emigrating from a place where a man cannot establish his religion. And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever flees with his religion from one land to another land, even if it be a span of earth, Paradise becomes due to him, and he will be a companion of his father Abraham and his Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon them both."

﴿except the oppressed among men, women, and children﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception whose content does not belong to the same category as what precedes it), because they are not included in the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) and its pronoun, or in the demonstrative referring to it. Mentioning the children is clear if by them is meant the slaves. If by them is meant the young boys, the mention serves to emphasize the matter and to indicate that they are on the verge of being obligated to emigrate (*hijra*). For when they reach maturity and are able to emigrate, there is no escape for them from it, and their guardians must emigrate with them whenever that becomes possible. ﴿who have no means, and are not guided to a way﴾ is either a description of the oppressed, since no specific time is attached to it, or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from them or from the concealed pronoun within them. The ability to find a means (*istita'at al-hila*) is finding the causes of emigration and what depends upon them, and being guided to the way (*ihtida' al-sabil*) is knowing the road either by oneself or by a guide.

﴿So as for those, it may be that God will pardon them﴾ is expressed with the word of hope (*kalimat al-it'am*) and the word "pardon," as a notice that abandoning emigration is a grave matter, to the extent that the one compelled by necessity should not feel secure, but should watch for the opportunity and attach his heart to it. (p-93) ﴿And God is ever Pardoning, Forgiving.﴾

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 100:

﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance.﴾ (*Muraghaman*) meaning a place of movement away, from *al-righam*, which is dust (*al-turab*). It is also said: a path by which one causes his people distress through his conduct, that is, he leaves them in spite of their noses, and this too is from *al-righam*. (*Wasa'a*) means abundance in provision and the manifestation of the religion.

﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, and then death overtakes him﴾ It is also read *yudrikuhu* (with a *damma*) in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: then he, death overtakes him. And in the accusative, by the implied *an* (that), as in his saying:

*"I shall leave my dwelling among the Banu Tamim, and I shall join the Hijaz, and rest."*

﴿then his reward has become due from Allah, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ *Al-wuqu'* (occurrence) and *al-wujub* (obligation) are close in meaning, and the sense is: his reward is established with Allah, Exalted, with the firmness of a binding matter. This noble verse was revealed concerning Jundub ibn Damra. His sons carried him on a litter heading toward Medina, and when he reached al-Tan'im he was at the point of death. He clapped his right hand upon his left and said: "O Allah, this is for You and this is for Your Messenger. I pledge allegiance to You upon what Your Messenger (ﷺ) pledged to You upon." Then he died.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 101:

﴿And when you travel in the land﴾ (ḍarabtum fī al-arḍ), i.e., you journey. ﴿there is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer﴾ by halving its units (rakaʿat) and the removal of hardship in it indicates its permissibility (jawāz) rather than its obligation (wujūb). This is supported by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) would complete (his prayer) while on journey. «And that ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, performed ʿumrah with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I shortened (the prayer) and completed it, I fasted and broke my fast." He said: "You have done well, O ʿĀ'isha."»

Abu Hanifa held it to be obligatory, based on the saying of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: «The prayer of travel is two rakʿat, complete and not shortened, on the tongue of your Prophet (ﷺ),» and on the saying of ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: «The prayer was first prescribed as two rakʿat, two rakʿat, then it was confirmed for travel and increased for residence.» Their apparent meaning contradicts the noble verse. If they are authentic, then the first is interpreted as meaning that it is like the complete (prayer) in validity and sufficiency, and the second does not negate the permissibility of increase, so there is no need to interpret the verse. [The reason is] that they had become accustomed to the four (rakʿat), so they were liable to think that the two rakʿat of travel were a shortening and deficiency; thus bringing them is called shortening according to their assumption. The negation of blame in it is so that their souls may be content with it. The shortest journey in which the prayer is shortened is four barids according to us, and six according to Abu Hanifa.

It was read as «tuqṣirū» from aqṣara, with the meaning of qaṣura, and «min al-ṣalāh» is an adjectival modifier of a deleted noun, i.e., "some of the prayer," according to Sibawayh; and the object of tuqṣirū is (taken as) an addition from Akhfash's view. ﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you; indeed the disbelievers are to you a clear enemy﴾ is a condition (sharīṭa) considered in terms of what is usual at that time, and for this reason its implicit converse (mafhūm) was not taken into account, just as it was not taken into account in His saying: ﴿And if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon them for what she gives up therewith﴾. The traditions have also widely established its permissibility in a state of security. It was read as «min al-ṣalāh an yaftinakum» without "in khiftum," meaning "lest they tempt you": that is, fighting and attacking with what is disliked.

(p-94) ﴿When you are among them and lead them in prayer﴾. Those who restrict the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf, the prayer performed in situations of danger) to being held in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ) because of the excellence of congregational prayer rely on its implied meaning. Most jurists (fuqahā', legal scholars) hold that Allah taught the Messenger (ﷺ) its manner so that the imams after him would follow it, since they are his deputies, and so their presence is like his presence. ﴿Let one group of them stand with you﴾: divide them into two groups, and let one of them stand with you while they pray, while the other group stands facing the enemy. ﴿And let them take their weapons﴾: that is, the worshippers should take precautions. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the other group, and the mention of the first group points to them. ﴿Then when they have prostrated﴾: that is, the worshippers. ﴿Then let them take their positions behind you﴾: that is, those who are not praying, guarding you, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ) and those praying with him. The addressee is thus used in place of the majority. ﴿And let another group who have not prayed come forward﴾, because they are occupied with guarding. ﴿And let them pray with you﴾. Its apparent meaning indicates that the imam prays twice, once with each group, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did at Batn Nakhl. If it is intended that he prays with each group one rak'ah, when the prayer is two rak'ahs, then the manner is that he prays the first rak'ah with the first group and remains standing while they complete their prayer alone and go to face the enemy, and the other group comes, and he completes the second rak'ah with them. Then he waits seated until they complete their prayer and he makes the salam with them, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did at Dhāt al-Riqā'. Abū Ḥanīfa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: he prays the first rak'ah with the first group, then they leave and stand facing the enemy, and the other group comes and prays one rak'ah with him, and he completes his prayer. Then they return to face the enemy, and the first group comes and performs the second rak'ah without recitation and completes their prayer, then they return and the other group comes and performs the rak'ah with recitation and completes their prayer. ﴿And let them take their precautions and their weapons﴾: caution (ḥidhr) has been made an instrument by which one fortifies oneself in battles, so it is joined with weapons in the obligation of taking them. A parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and those who had settled in the abode and in faith﴾, and ﴿The disbelievers wish that you would neglect your weapons and your belongings so that they could attack you in one single assault﴾. They wished to obtain an opportunity against you during your prayer, so that they could press upon you in one single assault. This explains the reason for which they were commanded to take precaution and to carry weapons. ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons because of rain that troubles you or if you are ill﴾: a concession to them to put them down when carrying them becomes burdensome because of rain or illness. This supports the view that the command to take them is for obligation and not for recommendation. ﴿And take your precaution﴾: He commanded them, despite this, to take precaution so that the enemy would not attack them unexpectedly. ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾: a promise to the believers of victory over the disbelievers after the command to be cautious, so that their hearts would be strengthened, and so that they would know that the command to be cautious is not because of their weakness or the enemy's dominance, but because it is obligatory to observe, in matters, the customs of vigilance and deliberation, and then to put their trust in Allah, glorified is He and exalted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 103:

﴿So when you have finished the prayer (ṣalāh)﴾ — that is, when you have performed it and completed it. ﴿Remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on your sides﴾ — so persist in remembrance (dhikr) in all circumstances; or, when you intend to perform the prayer while fear is intense, then perform it in whatever manner is possible: standing, fighting with swords and engaging in combat, sitting, shooting arrows, and lying on your sides, wounded. ﴿And when you are secure﴾ — when your hearts have calmed from fear. ﴿Then establish the prayer﴾ — so make it balanced, observe its pillars (arkān) and conditions (sharā'iṭ), and perform it complete. ﴿Indeed, prayer has been enjoined upon the believers at fixed times﴾ — an obligation with prescribed times, which may not be delayed beyond its times under any circumstances. This is evidence that the intended meaning of "remembrance" is the prayer, and that it must be performed during the fighting and turmoil of battle; and it is a reason (ta'līl) for the command to perform it in whatever manner is possible. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the one who is fighting does not pray until he is at ease.

(p-95) ﴿And do not falter﴾: do not weaken. ﴿in pursuit of the people﴾: in seeking out the disbelievers for fighting. ﴿If you are suffering, then they too are suffering as you suffer, and you hope from Allah for what they do not hope﴾: this is a binding argument against them and a rebuke for their laxity in it, since the harm of fighting falls upon both parties and is not specific to them; and they hope from Allah, through it, for the manifestation of the religion and the earning of rewards, which their enemy does not hope for. Therefore they should be more eager than them for war and more patient in it. It has also been read as «أنْ تَكُونُوا» (an takūnū, with a fatḥah), meaning "and do not falter because you are suffering" (ولا تهنوا لأن تكونوا تألمون); in this reading, his saying ﴿for they suffer﴾ serves as the cause (ʿillah, reason) for the prohibition against faltering on account of it. The verse was revealed concerning Badr al-Ṣughrā (the Lesser Badr). ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of your deeds and your inner thoughts. ﴿Wise﴾ in what He commands and forbids.

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book with the truth, that you may judge between the people﴾. It was revealed concerning Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq of the Banu Zafar. He stole a coat of mail from his neighbour Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man, hiding it in a bag of flour. The flour kept scattering through a hole in the bag, and he concealed the coat of mail with Zayd ibn al-Samin, a Jew. The coat of mail was sought from Tu'mah but was not found, and he swore that he had not taken it and had no knowledge of it. So they left him and followed the trail of the flour until it led to the Jew's house, and they took the coat of mail from there. The Jew said: Tu'mah gave it to me. Some people from among the Jews testified on his behalf. The Banu Zafar said: Come with us to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They asked him to argue on behalf of their companion, and they said: If you do not do so, he will be ruined and disgraced, and the Jew will be cleared. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was inclined to do so, "by what God has shown you," meaning by what God has made you know and revealed to you. "Shown" here is not in the sense of knowledge, for otherwise it would require three objects (mafa'il, the grammatical objects of a verb).

﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾, that is, do not argue for their sake or defend them, ﴿a disputant﴾ on behalf of the innocent.

﴿And seek forgiveness of God﴾ for what you were inclined to do. ﴿Indeed, God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ to whoever seeks His forgiveness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 107–108:

﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ — they betray themselves (yakhunūnahā). For the harm of their betrayal returns upon themselves. Or He made sin a betrayal of themselves, just as it was made an injustice to themselves. The pronoun refers to Ṭu'ma and his like, or to him and his people, for they shared in the sin when they testified to his innocence and disputed on his behalf. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love one who is a habitual betrayer﴾ — exaggerating in betrayal, persisting in it. ﴿Sinful﴾ — immersed in it.

It is narrated: Ṭu'ma fled to Makkah, apostatized, and breached a wall there in order to steal from its people, and the wall fell upon him and killed him.

﴿They conceal [themselves] from people﴾ — they hide from them out of shame and fear. ﴿But they do not conceal [themselves] from Allah﴾ — they are not ashamed before Him, and He is more worthy that He be shamed before and feared. ﴿And He is with them﴾ — their secret is not hidden from Him, so there is no way with Him except to abandon what He detests and what He holds them accountable for. ﴿When they plot﴾ — they devise and fabricate. ﴿what He does not approve of in speech﴾ — such as slandering the innocent, false oaths, and false testimony. ﴿And Allah is ever encompassing of what they do﴾ — nothing escapes Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 109–110:

﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world⦈ — "Here you are" (ha antum ha'ulaa') is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). ﴿You argued on their behalf in the life of this world⦈ is a clause explaining the occurrence of "these" (ulaa') as the predicate, or as a relative clause (silah) according to those who take it as a relative pronoun (mawsul). ﴿Who then will argue with God on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian (wakil)?⦈ — a defender (muhami) who would protect them from the punishment of God.

(p-96) ﴿And whoever does an evil⦈ — an ugly deed whose harm reaches others. ﴿Or wrongs himself⦈ — by that which is confined to him and does not extend beyond him. It has been said that by "evil" (su') is meant what falls short of shirk, and by "wronging" (zulm) is meant shirk. It has also been said: the minor and the major sins. ﴿Then seeks God's forgiveness⦈ — through repentance. ﴿He will find God Forgiving⦈ of his sins, ﴿Merciful⦈ — bestowing favour upon him. In this there is an exhortation to Ta'mah and his people to repent and seek forgiveness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 111–112:

﴿And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself﴾, so its consequence does not go beyond him, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you do evil, it is for yourselves﴾. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾, meaning He is Knowing of His act and Wise in recompensing it. ﴿And whoever earns a fault﴾, a minor sin, or that which is not committed deliberately. ﴿Or a sin﴾, a major sin, or that which is committed deliberately. ﴿Then throws it onto an innocent person﴾, as Ta'mah threw it onto Zayd, and He used the singular pronoun because of the position of "aw" (or). ﴿Then he has taken upon himself a slander and a manifest sin﴾, by means of throwing the innocent person and clearing the sinful self, and for this reason He equated the two, even though the perpetrator of one of them is not the perpetrator of the other.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 113:

﴿And were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy﴾ by informing you, through revelation, of what they were planning. The pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿A group of them would have been determined﴾ — that is, of the Banu Zafar. ﴿to lead you astray﴾ from judging by the truth, while they knew the situation. The clause is the response (jawab) to "were it not" (lawla), and the intent is not to negate their determination but to negate its effect upon you. ﴿But they do not lead astray except themselves﴾ because it did not divert you from the truth, and its consequence returns upon them. ﴿And they cannot harm you in anything﴾ for Allah, glorified and exalted, has protected you. What occurred to your mind was reliance on the apparent matter, not an inclination in the ruling. The word "min shay'" (in anything) is in the accusative position as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "any part of harm." ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you did not know﴾ of hidden matters, or of the affairs of the religion and its rulings. ﴿And the bounty of Allah upon you has been tremendous﴾, since there is no greater bounty than prophethood.

**"There is no good in much of their secret talk"** (﴿لا خَيْرَ في كَثِيرٍ مِن نَجْواهُمْ﴾). Here "their secret talk" may refer to the people engaged in it (*mutanajiyihim*), as in His saying: ﴿And when they hold secret counsel﴾ (﴿وَإذْ هم نَجْوى﴾). Or it may refer to the act of conferring secretly (*tanajihim*). Then His saying, ﴿except for one who enjoins charity or what is right﴾ (﴿إلا مَن أمَرَ بِصَدَقَةٍ أوْ مَعْرُوفٍ﴾), is elided with an omitted noun, meaning "except the secret talk of one who enjoins...". Or it is an exception of disconnection (*al-inqita'*), in the sense of "but as for one who enjoins charity, there is good in his secret talk."

The *ma'ruf* (what is right, the approved good) is everything that the Sacred Law (*al-shar'*) approves and that reason does not reject. Here it is interpreted as lending, relieving the distressed (*ighathat al-malhuf*), voluntary charity, and all else that has been interpreted in this way.

﴿or the reconciling of people﴾ (﴿أوْ إصْلاحٍ بَيْنَ النّاسِ﴾), or the reconciling of hearts (*islah dhat al-bayn*).

﴿And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of God, We shall give him a great reward﴾ (﴿وَمَن يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ ابْتِغاءَ مَرْضاتِ اللَّهِ فَسَوْفَ نُؤْتِيهِ أجْرًا عَظِيمًا﴾). The statement is built upon the imperative (*al-amr*), and the reward is arranged upon the act, to indicate that when the one who enjoins has entered the company of the good, the doer is more entitled to be counted among them. The principal matter and purpose is the act itself, and the enjoining is considered only insofar as it is a means leading to it. The act is restricted by the intention to seek the pleasure of God, glorified and exalted is He, because actions are by intentions, and whoever does good for show and reputation does not deserve a reward from God for it. The reward is described as great to alert to the insignificance of what is lost of the worldly goods that are sacrificed for it.

Hamzah and Abu 'Amr read *yu'tihi* with the *ya'* (third person, "We shall give him" becomes "He shall give him").(p-97)

﴿Whoever opposes the Messenger﴾ contradicts him. It is from *al-shaqq* (the side), for each of two opponents is on a side other than the other's side. ﴿After the guidance has become clear to him﴾ the truth has become manifest to him through encountering the miracles. ﴿And follows other than the way of the believers﴾ other than what they hold of belief or practice. ﴿We will turn him to what he has turned to﴾ We will make him governed by the misguidance he has turned to, and leave him between himself and what he has chosen. ﴿And burn him in Hell﴾ and We will cause him to enter it. It has also been read with an opening *fatha* on the *nun* (*nusli*), from *salah* (burning). ﴿And evil is it as a destination﴾ Hell.

The verse indicates the prohibition of opposing the consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement), because Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, attached the severe threat to opposing the Messenger and following other than the way of the believers. This is either because each of the two is individually forbidden, or one of them is, or their combination is. The second possibility is invalid, since it would be absurd to say that whoever drinks wine and eats bread deserves the *hadd* (the prescribed punishment). The third is likewise, because opposing [the Messenger] is forbidden whether or not something else is added to it. And if following other than their way is forbidden, then following their way is obligatory, because abandoning the way of the believers, for one who knows their way, amounts to following other than their way. I have fully explored this matter in *Mirsad al-Afham ila Mabadi al-Ahkam* (*The Observatory of Understandings Toward the Foundations of Rulings*).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 116:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whomever He wills.﴾ He repeated it for emphasis, or because of the story of Ta'mah. It was also said: "A old man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'I am an old man immersed in sins, except that I have not associated anything with Allah since I came to know Him and believed in Him, I have not taken any protector besides Him, I have not committed acts of disobedience out of audacity, and I did not imagine for the blink of an eye that I could escape Allah by flight. I am regretful and repentant, so what is my state with Allah, glorified and exalted be He?' Then it was revealed: ﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah has certainly strayed far astray.﴾" It means astray from the truth, for associating partners is the greatest kind of misguidance and the farthest from correctness and uprightness. In the first verse he mentioned "has indeed fabricated" (fa-qad iftara) because it is connected to the story of the People of the Book, and the origin of their association was a kind of fabrication, namely the claim of adoption against Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 117:

﴿In yad'una min dunihi illa inathan﴾ (They invoke, apart from Him, only females). He means al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat and the like. Each tribe had an idol which they worshipped and called "the female of Banu so-and-so." This was either because their names were feminine, as in the verse:

Wa ma dhakarun fa-in yasman fa-unthā * shadīd al-azm laysa lahu durus

(And a male, if it grows fat, becomes a female, hard-jointed, having no molars.)

He meant the tick (quraad), which when small is called quraad and when grown is called halama. Or it is because they were inanimate objects (jamadat), and inanimate things are made feminine inasmuch as they resemble females in having no benefit of their own. Perhaps Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned them by this name as an indication that they worship what they call females, because it is acted upon and does not act, whereas the one worshipped by right should be an agent, not one acted upon, so that this would be evidence of the extreme of their ignorance and the excess of their folly. It was also said that the intended meaning is the angels, because of their saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah, glorified and exalted." It is the plural of unthā, like rabāb and ruba. It was also read as "unthā" in the singular, and "unuthan" as the plural of anīth, like khubthā and khabīth. And "wuthunan" with light and heavy pronunciation, which is the plural of wathan, like asad and usud and usd. And "uthunan" and "uthnan" with both, by changing the waw because of its vowel into a hamza.

﴿wa in yad'una﴾ (and they do not invoke) i.e., and they do not worship by worshipping them. ﴿illa shaytanan marīdan﴾ (except a rebellious devil), because he is the one who commanded them to worship them and incited them to it, so their obedience to him in that is as worship of him. Al-marid and al-marid are the one who does not cling to good. The root meaning of the form is adherence (mulabasa). From it come sarh mumarrad (a smoothed palace), ghulam amrad (a beardless youth), and shajara marda' (a tree whose leaves have fallen off).

﴿Whom Allah cursed﴾ is a second attribute of Satan. ﴿And he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion"﴾ is coordinated with it, meaning: a rebellious Satan who combines the curse of Allah, and this statement indicates his extreme enmity toward mankind.

First, Allah, glorified and exalted be He, proved on the basis of causation that polytheism (shirk) is utter misguidance, because what they associate with Him is acted upon and does not perform a voluntary act. This runs entirely contrary to divinity (uluhiyyah), since the God should be an agent, not one acted upon. Then He argued that worshipping Satan is the most abominable misguidance, on three grounds.

The first: he is a rebellious one, fully immersed in misguidance, attached to no good or guidance, so obeying him is far-reaching misguidance, distant from guidance.

The second: he is cursed for his misguidance, so obeying him brings nothing but misguidance and cursing.

The third: he is in the utmost enmity and striving to destroy them, and allying oneself with one of such a nature is the height of misguidance, let alone worshipping him.

Al-mafrud means the cut off, determined; that is, a portion decreed for me. It derives from their saying, "He appointed (faraḍa) for him a share in the gift."

﴿And I will mislead them﴾ from the truth. ﴿And I will arouse in them false desires﴾, such as the length of life and the belief that there is no resurrection and no punishment.

﴿And I will command them, so they will slit the ears of the cattle﴾, cutting them so as to forbid what God has permitted. This is an expression for what the Arabs used to do with the *baḥā'ir* (she-camels whose ears were slit and which were released, and whose milk was forbidden) and the *sawā'ib* (animals released for their idols). It also points to the forbidding of what God has permitted and to the diminishing of everything He created complete, whether in actuality or in potential. ﴿And I will command them, so they will change the creation of God﴾, altering its form, its shape, or its attributes. Included in this is what has been said about gouging out the eye of the *ḥāmī* (a stallion camel set free), castrating slaves, tattooing, *al-washr* (filing the teeth), sodomy, lesbianism, and the like; worshipping the sun and the moon; altering the *fiṭrah* (the natural disposition) of God, which is Islam; and using the limbs and faculties for what does not return to the self as perfection and does not bring it nearness to God, glory be to Him, and exalted is He.

The generality of the wording prohibits castration absolutely, but the jurists (*fuqahā'*) permitted the castration of animals when there is a need. The four clauses are a report of what Satan said, whether by speech or by his action. ﴿And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of God﴾, by preferring what he calls to over what God has commanded, and by turning away from obedience to God, glory be to Him, and exalted is He, toward obedience to him. ﴿Then he has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾, if he has squandered his capital and exchanged, in its place, a station in Paradise for a station in the Fire.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 120–121:

﴿He promises them﴾: what He will not fulfil. ﴿And arouses their desires﴾: what they will not attain. ﴿And Satan promises them nothing but delusion﴾: and this is the showing of benefit in what contains harm. This promise is either through corrupt suggestions (al-khawatir al-fasida), or through the tongues of his allies (awliya'ihi).

﴿Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will not find from it any escape﴾: a place of deviation (ma'dil) and a place of flight (mahrab), from haṣa (yahis) meaning he deviated (idha 'adala). ﴿From it﴾ (ʿanha) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it (the subject, i.e., from maḥīṣ), and it is not a complement (ṣila) for it, because it is a noun of place (ism makan). And even if it is made a verbal noun (masdar), it does not govern what precedes it.
