Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 122:

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We shall admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true.﴾ That is, His promise is a promise, and the truth of that is truth (ḥaqqan). The first (waʿd Allāh, "the promise of Allah") is an emphatic (mu'akkid) for itself, because the meaning of the nominal sentence preceding it is a promise; and the second (ḥaqqan) is an emphatic for something other than itself. It is also permissible for the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl, here "those who") to be in the accusative governed by a verb that is explained by what follows it. The promise of Allah is by His saying "We shall admit them," because it means "We promise them admission (to the gardens)." And ḥaqqan is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the verbal noun (maṣdar).

﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ This is an emphatic and eloquent sentence. The purpose of the verse is to counter the false satanic promises made to his associates with the true promise of Allah to His allies, and the intensification of its emphasis is an encouragement for the servants to attain it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 123:

﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book.﴾ That is: the reward that Allah has promised is not attained by your wishful thinking, O Muslims, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; it is attained only by faith (iman) and righteous action (amal salih). It has also been said: faith is not by mere wishing (tamanni), but it is what settles in the heart and is confirmed by action.

It has been narrated: "(The Muslims and the People of the Book boasted. The People of the Book said: 'Our prophet came before your prophet, our scripture came before your scripture, and we are more deserving of Allah than you.' The Muslims said: 'We are more deserving than you. Our prophet is the Seal of the Prophets, and our scripture abrogates (yaqdi 'ala) the earlier scriptures.' So this was revealed.)"

It has also been said: the address is to the polytheists, and this is indicated by their being mentioned earlier. That is: the matter is not by the wishful thinking of the polytheists, which is their saying, "There is no Paradise and no Hellfire," and their saying, "If the matter is as these people claim, we will surely be better than them and in a better state." Nor is it by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book, which is their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ and their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few countable days﴾. Then He affirmed this and said: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾, whether in this world or in the next, because of what has been narrated: "(When it was revealed, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Then who will be saved with this, O Messenger of Allah?' The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Do you not grieve? Do you not fall ill? Does not affliction (al-la'wa') befall you?' He said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'That is it.')"

﴿And he will not find for himself, besides Allah, any protector or helper.﴾ That is, if he goes beyond the guardianship and support of Allah, he will not find for himself anyone who will be his protector or helper in repelling the punishment from him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 124:

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾ — some of them, or some part of them. For no one is able to do all of them, nor is he obligated to do all of them.

﴿whether male or female﴾ — this is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "yaʿmal" (does). The min here is either explanatory (li-l-bayān), so that "min al-ṣāliḥāt" means "being of male or female," or it is the min of beginning (li-l-ibtidāʾ).

﴿while he is a believer﴾ — a circumstantial clause. Joining the deed with faith is made a condition for obtaining the mentioned reward, and it is a reminder that no deed is counted without it.

﴿those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged a speck (naqīr)﴾ — by any reduction of the reward. And if the reward of the obedient is not reduced, then it is all the more fitting that the punishment of the disobedient not be increased, because the One who recompenses is the Most Merciful of the merciful. For this reason he limited the mention to the reward alone (lit. he restricted it to mentioning it after the reward).

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Abu Bakr recited "yudkhalūna al-Janna" here and in Ghafir and Maryam with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the khāʾ (yudkhalūna), while the rest recited it with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the khāʾ (yadkhulūna).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 125–126:

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God﴾ — he sincerely devotes his self (nafs) to God, knowing no lord for it other than Him. It was also said: he yields his face to Him in prostration. In this interrogative form there is an alert that this is the furthest point that human capacity can reach. ﴿And he is a doer of good﴾ — one who performs good deeds and abstains from evil deeds. ﴿And follows the religion (millah) of Abraham﴾ — the creed agreeing with the religion of Islam, whose soundness is agreed upon, ﴿a hanif﴾ — inclining away from all other religions. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the one who follows, or from the religion (millah), or from Abraham. ﴿And God took Abraham as a khalil (intimate friend)﴾ — He chose him and singled him out with an honour resembling the honour of a close friend with his friend. The reason he repeated the name rather than using a pronoun is to magnify his status and to specify that he is the one being praised. The khullah (intimacy) derives from khilal (interspersion), since it is a love that penetrates the soul and mingles with it. It was also said it derives from khalal (gap), since each of the two intimates fills the other's gap; or from al-khall, the track in the sand, since the two of them travel the same path; or from al-khallah in the sense of khaslah (quality), since the two agree in their qualities. The sentence is a new clause (isti'naf), brought to encourage following his religion, ﷺ, and to announce that it is the culmination of goodness and the ultimate perfection of humankind.

It was narrated: "(That Abraham, peace be upon him, sent to a khalil of his in Egypt during a famine that struck the people, to obtain food (yamtar) from him. His khalil said: 'If Abraham wanted it for himself I would have done it, but he wants it for the guests, and we too have been struck by what has struck the people.' Then his servants passed by a soft plain (batha'ah layyinah) and filled sacks with it out of shame before the people. When they informed Abraham, the news displeased him, and his eyes overcame him so he slept. Sarah got up to a sack of it, took out fine flour (huwwarah) and baked bread. Abraham, peace be upon him, awoke and smelled the scent of bread and said: 'From where do you have this?' She said: 'From your Egyptian khalil.' He said: 'Rather, it is from my khalil, God, Mighty and Majestic.' So God named him khalil.)"

﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾ — in creation and ownership; He chooses from them whom He wills and what He wills. It was also said that it is connected to the mention of the workers, affirming the obligation of obedience to Him upon the people of the heavens and the earth, and the perfection of His power to recompense them for their deeds.

﴿And God is ever, of all things, encompassing﴾ — with an encompassing of knowledge and power; so He is knowing of their deeds and will recompense them for their good and their evil.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 125–126:

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God﴾ — he sincerely devotes his self (nafs) to God, knowing no lord for it other than Him. It was also said: he yields his face to Him in prostration. In this interrogative form there is an alert that this is the furthest point that human capacity can reach. ﴿And he is a doer of good﴾ — one who performs good deeds and abstains from evil deeds. ﴿And follows the religion (millah) of Abraham﴾ — the creed agreeing with the religion of Islam, whose soundness is agreed upon, ﴿a hanif﴾ — inclining away from all other religions. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the one who follows, or from the religion (millah), or from Abraham. ﴿And God took Abraham as a khalil (intimate friend)﴾ — He chose him and singled him out with an honour resembling the honour of a close friend with his friend. The reason he repeated the name rather than using a pronoun is to magnify his status and to specify that he is the one being praised. The khullah (intimacy) derives from khilal (interspersion), since it is a love that penetrates the soul and mingles with it. It was also said it derives from khalal (gap), since each of the two intimates fills the other's gap; or from al-khall, the track in the sand, since the two of them travel the same path; or from al-khallah in the sense of khaslah (quality), since the two agree in their qualities. The sentence is a new clause (isti'naf), brought to encourage following his religion, ﷺ, and to announce that it is the culmination of goodness and the ultimate perfection of humankind.

It was narrated: "(That Abraham, peace be upon him, sent to a khalil of his in Egypt during a famine that struck the people, to obtain food (yamtar) from him. His khalil said: 'If Abraham wanted it for himself I would have done it, but he wants it for the guests, and we too have been struck by what has struck the people.' Then his servants passed by a soft plain (batha'ah layyinah) and filled sacks with it out of shame before the people. When they informed Abraham, the news displeased him, and his eyes overcame him so he slept. Sarah got up to a sack of it, took out fine flour (huwwarah) and baked bread. Abraham, peace be upon him, awoke and smelled the scent of bread and said: 'From where do you have this?' She said: 'From your Egyptian khalil.' He said: 'Rather, it is from my khalil, God, Mighty and Majestic.' So God named him khalil.)"

﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾ — in creation and ownership; He chooses from them whom He wills and what He wills. It was also said that it is connected to the mention of the workers, affirming the obligation of obedience to Him upon the people of the heavens and the earth, and the perfection of His power to recompense them for their deeds.

﴿And God is ever, of all things, encompassing﴾ — with an encompassing of knowledge and power; so He is knowing of their deeds and will recompense them for their good and their evil.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 127:

﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women.﴾ About their inheritance. The occasion of its revelation was that ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "We have been informed that you give the daughter half and the sister half, whereas we used to give inheritance only to those who fight in battle and take the spoils." He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Thus I have been commanded."

﴿Say: God gives you a ruling concerning them.﴾ He makes clear to you His ruling concerning them. Ifta' (issuing a legal ruling) is the clarification of what is ambiguous. ﴿And what is recited to you in the Book﴾ is conjoined to the name of God, the Exalted, or to the pronoun concealed in yuftikum (gives you a ruling). It is permissible because of the separation, so that the giving of the ruling is ascribed to God, glory be to Him, and also to what is in the Qur'an, such as His saying: "God enjoins you..." and the like. One verb may be attributed to two different agents under two different considerations, and its parallel is: "Zayd has enriched me, and his gift." Or it is a parenthetical resumptive clause, to magnify what is recited to them, with "what is recited to you in the Book" being a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is "in the Book." The intended meaning of "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet. It may also be read in the accusative, on the sense of "and He makes clear to you what is recited to you," or in the genitive, on the basis of an oath, as if it were said: "And I swear by what is recited to you in the Book." It is not permissible to conjoin it to the genitive noun in fihinna, because that is faulty both in wording and in meaning.

﴿Concerning the orphan women﴾ is a relative clause for yutla (is recited), if the relative pronoun is conjoined to what precedes it, meaning: "what is recited to you concerning their affair." Otherwise it is a substitute (badal) for fihinna, or another relative clause for yuftikum, in the sense: "God gives you a ruling concerning them by reason of the orphan women," just as you say: "I spoke to you today about Zayd." This idiomatic phrase carries the meaning of min (from/concerning), because it is the attribution of a thing to its genus. It is also read as yayama, with two yāʾs, on the basis that it was ayama, and its hamza was changed to yāʾ.

﴿To whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them﴾, that is, what has been decreed for them of the inheritance. ﴿And you desire to marry them﴾, meaning: "in marrying them" or "from marrying them." The guardians of orphans used to desire them if they were beautiful and consume their wealth; and if not, they would prevent them from marrying out of greed for their inheritance. The waw may be taken as a circumstantial clause (hal) or as a conjunction (ʿatf). There is no evidence in this for the permissibility of marrying an orphan girl, since desire to marry her does not necessarily entail that the contract takes place while she is a minor.

﴿And the weak among the children﴾ is conjoined to "orphan women." The Arabs did not give inheritance to them, just as they did not give inheritance to women. ﴿And that you stand up for the orphans with justice﴾ is likewise conjoined to it, meaning: "and He gives you a ruling, or what is recited concerning your standing up [for them]." This is when you make fi yataba a relative clause for one of them; but if you make it a substitute, then the correct reading is to put both in the accusative, conjoined to the position of fihinna. It is also permissible to read "and that you stand up" in the accusative by supposing a verb, meaning: "and He commands you that you stand up," and this is an address to the rulers, that they look after them and secure their rights, or to those who uphold justice in their affairs.

﴿And whatever good you do, indeed God is ever Knowing of it.﴾ This is a promise to those who prefer good in this matter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 128:

﴿And if a woman fears ill-treatment or aversion from her husband﴾ she anticipates it from him because of the signs that have appeared to her; and "woman" (imra'a) is the agent of a verb whose meaning is explained by what follows it.

﴿ill-treatment (nushuz)﴾ turning away from her and disdaining her company, out of dislike for her and withholding her rights. ﴿Or aversion (i'rad)﴾ by his reducing his sitting with her and his conversing with her. ﴿There is no blame upon them both if they make a settlement between themselves, a settlement﴾ that they reconcile, by her remitting to him part of the dower or of her turn (al-qasm), or by her giving him something to win him over. The Kufans read "yuslihā" from aslaha (to make peace between disputing parties), and on this reading "sulhan" may be in the accusative as the object, with "baynahumā" being an adverbial of place or a circumstantial, or as a verbal noun (masdar), as in the first reading; the object of "baynahumā" is either implied or omitted. It has also been read "yuslihā" from aslaha in the sense of istalaha (to reach agreement). ﴿And settlement is better﴾ than separation, or than a bad marital life, or than enmity. It is not permissible that this be taken as a comparison of preference; rather it is a statement that it is among the goods, just as enmity is among the evils. This is a parenthetical remark (i'tiraD), and likewise His saying: ﴿And souls are made to be prone to stinginess﴾. For this reason the lack of congruence between the two is tolerated: the first is to encourage reconciliation, and the second is to prepare an excuse for haggling. The meaning of "the souls being made present to stinginess" is making them present to it and imprinted with it, so that a woman hardly consents to her husband turning away from her and falling short in her rights, nor does a man consent to keeping her and fulfilling her rights as he should if he dislikes her or loves another. ﴿And if you do good﴾ in companionship, ﴿and fear Allah﴾ by avoiding ill-treatment, aversion, and diminishing of rights, ﴿then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do﴾ of good and of contention, ﴿Acquainted (khabir)﴾, Knowing of it and of the purpose behind it, so He will recompense you for it. He has placed His knowing of their deeds in the position of rewarding them for them, which in reality is the answer of the conditional, establishing the cause in the place of the effect.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 129–130:

﴿And you will never be able to be just between wives﴾ because justice is that there should be no inclination whatsoever, and this is unattainable. Therefore, "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to divide [his time] among his wives and act justly, and he would say: 'This is my division in what I control, so do not blame me for what You control and I do not control.'"

﴿And even if you should strive﴾ i.e., to seek that and exert yourselves in it. ﴿Then do not incline completely﴾ by abandoning what is within your capacity and oppressing the one who is neglected, for what cannot be fully attained should not be wholly abandoned. ﴿And leave her suspended like one who is neither married nor divorced.⁠﴾ (i.e., the one who is neither a wife with a husband nor a divorcee).

And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever has two wives and inclines toward one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one of his sides leaning."

﴿And if you amend⁠﴾ what you had been corrupting of their affairs. ﴿and fear Allah⁠﴾ regarding what lies ahead of time. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful⁠﴾ — He will forgive you what has passed of your inclination.

﴿And if they separate⁠﴾ — it was also read as "wa in yatafaraqa" — i.e., if each of them parts from the other. ﴿Allah will enrich each⁠﴾ of them from the other with a substitute or consolation. ﴿from His abundance⁠﴾ — His wealth and His power. ﴿And ever is Allah Expansive and Wise⁠﴾ — Capable, and Precise in His actions and His rulings.

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, an alert to the perfection of His vastness and power. ﴿And We have certainly enjoined those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians, and those before them. The word *al-kitab* (the Scripture) is generic (*li-l-jins*, denoting the category as a whole). The phrase *min* (from) is connected either to *wassayna* (We enjoined) or to *utu* (were given). The context of the verse is to emphasize the command to sincerity (*ikhlas*). ﴿And you﴾ is conjoined (*ʿatf*) to *alladhina* (those). ﴿That fear Allah﴾ means *bi-an* (that), that is, "fear Allah." It is also permissible for *an* to be explanatory (*mufassira*), since the enjoining carries the sense of saying. ﴿But if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in (p-102) the earth﴾ is in the sense of "saying": that is, "We said to them and to you: if you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is the Owner of the entire dominion. He is not harmed by your disbelief and disobedience, just as He is not benefited by your gratitude and piety. He enjoined you only out of His mercy, not out of need." Then He confirmed this with His words: ﴿And Allah is ever Free of need﴾ from the creation and their worship, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ in His essence, whether or not He is praised.

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is mentioned a third time to indicate that He is Free of need and Praiseworthy. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 133–134:

﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people,﴾ meaning: destroy you. The object of "wills" (yasha') is omitted, being indicated by the apodosis (jawab). ﴿And bring others﴾ meaning: He will produce another people in your place, or other creatures in place of humankind. ﴿And God is capable of that﴾ of annihilation and bringing into being. ﴿Powerful﴾ possessing consummate power, such that nothing He wills is beyond Him. This is also an affirmation of His self-sufficiency and power, and a threat to those who disbelieve in Him and oppose His command. It is said that this is an address to those among the Arabs who opposed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and its meaning is the same as His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people other than you﴾, according to what is narrated: "When it was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) struck his hand on the back of Salman and said: 'They are the people of this one.'"

﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world﴾ like the warrior who fights for booty. ﴿With God is the reward of this world and the Hereafter﴾ so why does he seek the lesser of the two? Let him seek both, like one who says: "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter." Or let him seek the nobler of the two, for whoever fights sincerely for God, glorified and exalted is He, the booty will not elude him, and he has in the Hereafter what is, in comparison to it, nothing at all. Or: ﴿with God is the reward of both abodes﴾, so He gives each what he desires, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth﴾, to the end of the verse. ﴿And God is ever Hearing, Seeing﴾, knowing of intentions, so He recompenses each according to his aim.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 135:

﴿O you who have believed, be persistent in upholding justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives.﴾ (Be persistent) constant in justice, striving to establish it. ﴿Witnesses for Allah﴾ bearing true testimony, you establish your testimonies for the sake of the Face of Allah, glorified and exalted be He; and this is a second predicate or a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿Even if it be against yourselves﴾ even if the testimony is against yourselves, by your acknowledging it, because testimony is a clarification of the truth, whether it is against oneself or against others. ﴿Or parents and relatives﴾ even if it is against your parents and relatives. ﴿Whether he be rich or poor﴾ (i.e., the one testified against, or each of the two: the one testified against and the one testified for). ﴿Do not refrain from establishing testimony, nor deviate in it out of partiality or compassion.﴾ ﴿Allah is more worthy of both﴾ of the rich and the poor, and of considering their interests. Had the testimony not been against them or for their benefit, He would not have prescribed it. This is the cause of the answer, and it has been placed in its stead. The pronoun in ﴿bihima﴾ refers to what is indicated by what was mentioned, namely the two categories of rich and poor, not to the individual, for otherwise it would have been singular. This is confirmed by the reading «Allahu awla bihim» (in the plural). ﴿So do not follow desire, lest you deviate﴾ lest you deviate from the truth, or out of aversion to your deviating from justice.

﴿And if you distort﴾ your tongues from testimony for the truth, or from the judgment of justice. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read it with a sukun on the lam, followed by two waws, the first of which is damma-vowelled and the second sukun. Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿wa-in talu﴾ with the meaning: and if you take charge of establishing the testimony and then discharge it. ﴿Or refuse﴾ to discharge it. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ so He will recompense you for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 136:

(p-103) ﴿O you who have believed﴾ is an address to the Muslims, or to the hypocrites, or to the believers among the People of the Book, since it is narrated that: "Ibn Salam and his companions said: 'O Messenger of God, we believe in you and your Book, and in Moses and the Torah, and in 'Uzayr, and we disbelieve in what is other than that.' So this was revealed."

﴿Believe in God and His Messenger, and the Book that He sent down upon His Messenger, and the Book that He sent down before﴾ — i.e., remain steadfast in faith in that and persevere in it; or, believe in it with your hearts as you have believed with your tongues; or, believe a general faith that encompasses the Books and the Messengers, for belief in some of them is like no belief at all. The first Book is the Qur'an and the second is the genus (of scriptures). Nafi' and the Kufans read ﴿alladhi nazzala﴾ and ﴿alladhi anzala﴾ with a fatha on the nun, the hamza and the zay, while the rest read them with a damma on the nun and the hamza and a kasra on the zay.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in God, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, and the Last Day﴾ — i.e., whoever disbelieves in any of these. ﴿Then he has strayed into far error﴾ — far from the goal, such that he is hardly likely to return to the right path.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 137:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ — meaning the Jews, who believed in Musa (Moses), upon him be peace. ﴿Then they disbelieved﴾ when they worshipped the calf. ﴿Then they believed﴾ after his (Musa's) return to them. ﴿Then they disbelieved﴾ in Isa (Jesus), upon him be peace. ﴿Then they increased in disbelief﴾ in Muhammad (ﷺ). Or, (the verse refers to) a people among whom apostasy was repeated, and then they persisted in disbelief and increased in persistent deviation. ﴿Allah would not forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path﴾, since it is far-fetched that they would repent of disbelief and remain steadfast in faith, for their hearts have been sealed with disbelief and their insight blinded to the truth. This is not (to say) that if they were to sincerely believe, it would not be accepted from them, nor would they be forgiven. The predicate of kana (to be) in such instances is omitted, and the lam (of purpose) is attached to it, like: "Allah would not be willing to forgive them."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 138–139:

﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that there is a painful punishment for them.﴾ This indicates that the verse concerns the hypocrites, who had outwardly believed but secretly disbelieved again and again, then increased in their persistence in hypocrisy and in corrupting the affair for the believers. Placing "give good news" (bashshir) in place of "warn" (andhir) is a mockery of them.

﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾ is in the accusative position, or in the nominative position as a dispraise, in the sense of "I mean those who" or "they are those who." ﴿Do they seek honour with them?﴾ That is, do they seek to be strengthened by their alliance? ﴿Indeed, all honour belongs to Allah﴾ No one gains strength except the one whom Allah makes mighty, and He has decreed honour for His allies, so He said: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger and to the believers.﴾ The honour of others is not regarded when it is attributed to them.

And He has already sent down to you in the Book (﴿وَقَدْ نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكم في الكِتابِ﴾), meaning the Qur'an. ʿĀṣim read *nazzala* (active voice), while the rest read *nuzzila* (passive voice), with the deputy of the subject (*al-qāʾim maqām fāʿilihi*) being the object. *An* (the lightened form of *inna*, *al-mukhaffafa*) is here, in "that when you hear the signs of Allah" (﴿أنْ إذا سَمِعْتُمْ آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾), and the meaning is that when you hear them. Being disbelieved in and mocked (﴿يُكْفَرُ بِها ويُسْتَهْزَأُ بِها﴾) are two circumstantial qualifiers (*ḥāl*) referring to the signs. They are included to restrict the prohibition on sitting with them in His saying: ﴿فَلا تَقْعُدُوا مَعَهم حَتّى يَخُوضُوا في حَدِيثٍ غَيْرِهِ﴾ ("So do not sit with them until they engage in a conversation other than it"), which is the answer to the condition, to the case where the one sitting with them is a mocker, a stubborn opponent, and not hoped to be guided. This is supported by the final clause (*al-ghāyah*) (p-104). This is a reminder of what was revealed to them in Mecca in His saying: ﴿وَإذا رَأيْتَ الَّذِينَ يَخُوضُونَ في آياتِنا فَأعْرِضْ عَنْهُمْ﴾ ("And when you see those who engage in discussion about Our signs, turn away from them"), and so on.

The pronoun in *maʿahum* ("with them") refers to the disbelievers implied by His saying "being disbelieved in and mocked." ﴿إنَّكم إذًا مِثْلُهُمْ﴾ ("Then indeed you would be like them") means in sin, because you are able to turn away from them and to denounce them, or in disbelief, if you are pleased with that. Or it is because those who sit with the people who engage in discussion about the Qur'an from among the rabbis were hypocrites. This is indicated by: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ جامِعُ المُنافِقِينَ والكافِرِينَ في جَهَنَّمَ جَمِيعًا﴾ ("Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell, all of them"), meaning those who sit and those with whom they sit. *Idhan* is nullified (*mulghāh*) because it falls between the subject and the predicate, and for this reason the verb is not mentioned after it. The singular form *mithluhum* is used because it functions like a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or because it is sufficient with the genitive construction referring to the plural. It was also read with a fatḥah, being built, because it is attached to a built word, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿مِثْلَ ما أنَّكم تَنْطِقُونَ﴾ ("like your speaking").

﴿Those who wait in ambush against you﴾ means those who await the occurrence of some event befalling you. It is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for "those who take," or an attribute (*ṣifah*) of "the hypocrites and the disbelievers," or a censure (*dhamm*) in the nominative or accusative, or a subject whose predicate is what follows.

﴿If you get a victory from God, they say: "Were we not with you?"﴾ meaning, supporting you. "Then give us a share of what you have taken as booty."

﴿And if the disbelievers have a share﴾ of the war, then it is alternating (*sijāl*), ﴿they say: "Did we not gain control over you?"﴾ That is, they say to the disbelievers: "Did we not defeat you and gain the ability to kill you, but we spared you?" *Istiḥwādh* means taking control. By analogy (*qiyās*) it should have been said *istaḥādha yastaḥīdhu istiḥādhatan*, but it came in accordance with the original form (*al-aṣl*), namely *istaḥwadha yastaḥwidhu istiḥwādhan*.

﴿And we prevented you from the believers﴾ by letting them down, by casting into them an imagination that made their hearts weak, and by slackening in supporting them, so let us share in what you have obtained. The victory of the Muslims was called *fatḥ* (opening) and the victory of the disbelievers was called *naṣīb* (share) because of the baseness of their portion, since it is confined to a worldly matter that quickly passes away.

﴿So God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and God will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ then, at that time, or in this world. By *sabīl* (way) is meant proof (*ḥujjah*). Our companions used this verse as evidence for the invalidity of a disbeliever buying a Muslim (as a slave). The Ḥanafiyyah (the Ḥanafī school) used it to argue that separation (*baynūnah*) occurs by apostasy itself, but this is weak, because it does not rule out that if he returns to faith before the waiting period (*'idda*) has elapsed, the separation would not occur.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 142–143:

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them.﴾ The discussion of this was already covered at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. ﴿And when they stand up for prayer, they stand up lazily.﴾ That is, burdened, like one compelled to do the action. It is also read as kusala (with a fatha), and both are plural forms of kaslan (lazy). ﴿They show off to the people﴾ so that they may make them think they are believers. The word murA'ah (showing off) is a form of mufa'alah used in the sense of tafil (intensification), like ni'am and na'im; or it is for reciprocity, since the one who shows off displays his deed to the one he is showing off to, and that person displays his approval of him. ﴿And they do not remember Allah except a little﴾ since the one who shows off does not act except in the presence of the one he is showing off to, and this is the least of his conditions; or because their remembrance with the tongue is little compared to remembrance with the heart. It has also been said: the intended meaning of remembrance is prayer. And it has been said: the remembrance in it, for they do not mention anything in it except takbir and taslim.

﴿Wavering between that﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw of "yurA'un" (they show off), like His saying "wa la yadhkurun" (and they do not remember), meaning: they show off to them while not remembering, wavering; or from the waw of "yadhkurun"; or it is in the accusative as a term of blame. The meaning: vacillating between faith and disbelief. From dhabdhabah, which is making a thing unsettled; its origin is the sense of driving away. It is also read with a kasrah on the dhal, meaning "yudhabdhibuna qulubahum" (they unsettle their hearts) or their religion, or "yatadhabdhabun" (they are unsettled), like their saying "salsala" in the sense of "tasalsala". It is also read with an unpointed dal, meaning they took to one path at one time and to another path at another time. ﴿Neither to these nor to those﴾ neither attributed to the believers nor to the disbelievers; or neither heading completely to either of the two groups. ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, you will not find for him any way﴾ to the truth and right course. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light.﴾

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 144:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾ for it is the practice and habit of the hypocrites, so do not imitate them. ﴿Do you wish to give Allah a clear authority against yourselves?﴾ That is, a clear proof, for their alliance with them is evidence of hypocrisy; or an authority by which He would impose His punishment upon you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 145–146:

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire.﴾ (al-dark al-asfal) is the stratum at the bottom of Jahannam. It is so because they are the most wicked of the disbelievers, since they added to their disbelief mockery of Islam and deception of the Muslims. As for his saying, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him: "Whoever has three traits is a hypocrite, even if he fasts, prays, and claims that he is a Muslim: whoever, when he speaks, lies; whoever, when he promises, breaks his promise; and whoever, when he is entrusted, betrays," and the like, it is by way of comparison and severe warning.

The seven levels of it are called darakat (degrees/levels) because they follow one another in succession, one above the other. The Kufans read it with a sukun on the rā' (darkah, as in al-satr and al-satar, being a dialect form), but the vocalized form (darak) is more preferred, because its plural is adraak. ﴿And you will not find for them a helper﴾ who will remove them from it.

﴿Except those who repent﴾ from hypocrisy. ﴿And reform﴾ what they corrupted of their secrets and their conditions during the state of hypocrisy. ﴿And hold fast to Allah﴾ and put their trust in Him, or adhere to His religion. ﴿And make their religion sincerely for Allah﴾, not intending by their obedience anything but His Face, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿Then those will be with the believers﴾ and counted among them in both abodes. ﴿And Allah will give the believers a great reward﴾, so they will share in it with them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 147:

﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ Does He seek to satisfy His rage through it, or to ward off some harm, or to bring about some benefit through it? He is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), exalted above benefit and harm. Rather, He punishes only the one who persists in his disbelief, because his persistence in it is like a bad temperament that leads to sickness. So when he removes it through faith and gratitude, and disowns it from himself, he is freed from its consequence. He mentioned gratitude first because the one who looks (at things) first perceives the blessing, and so gives thanks in a general way, then he examines carefully until he knows the Benefactor, and so he believes in Him. ﴿And Allah is Appreciative﴾ (Shakir), i.e., He rewards: He accepts the little and gives the abundant. ﴿Knowing﴾ (Alim) of the true worth of your gratitude and your faith.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 148–149:

﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged.﴾ This is an exception: the wronged person's public complaint, namely calling down (the curse) upon the wrongdoer and seeking redress from him.

It is narrated that a man was a guest of a people, but they did not feed him, so he complained about them, and he was rebuked for it. Then this verse was revealed. It has also been read as ﴿مَن ظَلَمَ﴾ (man zalama, "one who wronged"), in the active voice, in which case the exception is disconnected (munqati', i.e. an exception not of the same category, here meaning "but"): the sense is, "But the wrongdoer does what Allah does not like." ﴿And Allah is ever Hearing﴾ of the words of the wronged, ﴿Knowing﴾ of the wrongdoer.

﴿If you disclose good﴾ through obedience and righteousness, ﴿or conceal it﴾ or do it in secret, ﴿or pardon an evil﴾ done to you, there is no blame on you for it. What is intended here is the pardoning, and the mention of disclosing and concealing good is a preface to it; for this reason, he followed it with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent﴾, meaning: He greatly pardons the disobedient while having complete power to punish them, so you are more deserving of this. This is an exhortation to the wronged to pardon after he was given permission to seek redress, urging them toward noble character.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 150–151:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers﴾ by believing in Allah and disbelieving in His messengers.

﴿And they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾ We believe in some of the prophets and disbelieve in others of them. ﴿And they wish to adopt between that a way﴾ a middle course between faith and disbelief, and there is no intermediate position, since the truth does not admit of variation. Faith in Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is not complete except by faith in His messengers and affirmation of them in what they conveyed from Him, in detail or in summary. So the one who disbelieves in some of that is like the one who disbelieves in all of it in misguidance, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾

﴿Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾ They are the complete disbelievers; there is no regard for their faith in this case. ﴿Truly (ḥaqqan)﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid) for another verb, or an adjective of the infinitive of "the disbelievers," meaning: they are those who disbelieved with true disbelief, that is, certain and verified. ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 152:

﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not make any distinction between any of them﴾ — their opponents and counterparts. The word "between" (bayna) has entered upon "one of them" (ahad), which requires a plural sense, due to its generality, insofar as it occurs in a context of negation. ﴿Those — He will surely give them their promised rewards﴾. Its being prefaced with "sawfa" (surely/soon) is for emphasizing the promise and indicating that it will certainly come to pass, even if delayed. Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, and Qalun, on the authority of Yaʿqub, read it with the "ya'" (third person), by way of shifting the address (talwin al-khitab). ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾ of what has passed from them. ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them by multiplying their good deeds.

﴿They ask you, the People of the Book, to bring down to them a Book from heaven.﴾ It was revealed concerning the rabbis (*ahbar*) of the Jews, who said: "If you are truthful, bring us a Book from heaven all at once, as Moses (peace be upon him) brought the Torah (*al-Tawrah*)." It was also said that they meant a book written in a heavenly script on tablets, as the Torah was, or a book that we see with our own eyes as it descends, or a book addressed to us individually, stating that you are the Messenger of God. ﴿So they had asked Moses for something greater than that.﴾ This is the response (*jawab*) to an implied conditional clause (*shart muqaddar*), meaning: if you consider what they asked of you to be a great thing, then they had asked Moses (peace be upon him) for something greater than it. Although this question was asked by their forefathers, it is attributed to them because they held to their doctrine and followed their guidance. The meaning is that their root (*'irq*) is firmly established in this, and that what they proposed to you is not the first of their ignorances and fancies. ﴿Then they said: "Show us God openly."﴾ *Jahrah* means in plain sight, that is, "Show Him to us so that we see Him openly," or "openly and face to face with Him." ﴿So the thunderbolt (*al-sa'iqah*) seized them.﴾ It was a fire that came from the direction of heaven and destroyed them. ﴿For their wrongdoing.﴾ That is, because of their wrongdoing, which was their obstinacy and their questioning, of what is impossible in the state they were in; and this does not necessitate the impossibility of seeing God absolutely. ﴿Then they took the calf (as a god) after the clear proofs had come to them.﴾ This is the second offence, which their forefathers also committed. The "clear proofs" (*al-bayyinat*) are the miracles. It is not permissible to interpret them as the Torah, since it had not yet come to them. ﴿Yet We pardoned them for that, and gave Moses clear authority.﴾ That is, manifest dominion over them, when he commanded them to kill themselves as repentance for their taking of the calf.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 154:

﴿And We raised over them the Mount (Tur) because of their covenant﴾, that is, because of their covenant, so that they would accept it. ﴿And We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating"﴾, upon the tongue of Musa, while the Mount was overhanging them. ﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath"﴾, upon the tongue of Dawud, peace be upon him. It is possible that it refers to upon the tongue of Musa, when the mountain was overshadowing them, for he legislated the Sabbath, but the transgression in it and the transformation into apes through it occurred in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him. Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', recited ﴿la ta'dukoo﴾ (la ta'dū), on the basis that its original form is ﴿la tata'adduu﴾, so the taa' was assimilated into the daal. Qalun recited with the vowel of the ayn being concealed (ikhfa') and the daal being doubled (tashdid), and the transmission from him is with sukun. ﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾, upon that, which is their saying, "We heard and we obeyed."

Al-Baydawi's commentary on Surah 4, verse 155:

﴿So for their breaking their covenant﴾. That is: they opposed and broke it, so We did to them what We did because of their breaking it. The *ma* (redundant *ma*, an extra particle used for emphasis) is for emphasis, and the *ba'* (the preposition "for/because of") is connected to the deleted verb. It is also permissible for it to be connected to *harramna 'alayhim tayyibat* ("We forbade them good things"), so the prohibition is because of the breaking, and what is conjoined to it up to His saying *fa-bizulmin* ("for wrongdoing") is connected not to what *bal taba'a Allahu 'alayha* ("rather, Allah has sealed it") indicates, like *la yu'minun* ("they do not believe"), because that is a rejection of their saying *qulubuna ghulf* ("our hearts are uncovered"). Thus it belongs to the complement of *wa qawlihim* ("and their saying"), which is conjoined to the genitive noun, so it does not govern its preposition (*jarr*).

﴿And their disbelief in the signs of Allah﴾: in the Qur'an, or in what came in their Scripture.

﴿And their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying: "Our hearts are uncovered"﴾: *ghulf* means containers for knowledge, or [hearts] in coverings from what you call us to.

﴿Rather, Allah has sealed upon them because of their disbelief﴾: so He made them veiled from knowledge, or He forsook them and withheld from them the success to reflect upon the signs and to take heed of the admonitions.

﴿So they do not believe, except a few﴾: of them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam; or [it means] a little faith, since it is of no account because of its deficiency.

[Surah 4, verse 156] **"And for their disbelief"** — in (rejecting) Jesus, upon him be peace. It is conjoined with "for their disbelief" (in verse 155), since it is among the causes of the sealing (of hearts). Or it is conjoined with his saying "for their breaking of their covenant." It is also permissible that the whole of this and what is conjoined to it be conjoined to the whole of what precedes it, and the repetition of the mention of disbelief would then be a notice of the repetition of their disbelief, for they disbelieved in Moses, then in Jesus, then in Muhammad, upon them be peace.

**"And for their saying against Mary a tremendous slander"** — meaning, attributing to her fornication (zina).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 157–158:

﴿And their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah."﴾ That is, according to their claim. It is also possible that they said it mockingly, and its parallel is ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾. It may also be a fresh statement from Allah, the Exalted, praising him, or a placing of a good mention in the place of their foul mention.

﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them.﴾

It is narrated (that a group of Jews insulted him and his mother, so he invoked curses upon them, and Allah transformed them into apes and swine. The Jews then gathered to kill him, so Allah informed him that He would raise him to the heaven. He said to his companions, "Which of you is willing to have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed, crucified, and enters Paradise?" A man from among them stood up, and Allah cast upon him (p-108) his likeness, so he was killed and crucified. And it is said (he was a man who was a hypocrite toward him, who went out to guide them to him, so Allah cast his likeness upon him, and he was seized, crucified and killed), and it is said: (Tituanus the Jew entered a house in which he was, but did not find him, and Allah cast his likeness upon him. When he came out, they thought he was Jesus, so he was seized and crucified). Such things are among the marvels that are not deemed improbable in the time of prophethood. Allah, the Exalted, censured them only for what the discourse indicates of their audacity toward Allah, the Exalted, and their intention to kill His Prophet, who was supported by manifest miracles, and their boasting about it, not for their statement itself, which was according to their assumption. "Was made to appear" is a passive verb with a prepositional phrase as its subject, as if it were said: "rather, the resemblance occurred to them between Jesus and the one killed," or "in the matter," according to the view of one who said: no one was killed, but rumour of his killing spread and circulated among the people; or it refers to the pronoun of the one killed, because of the indication of ﴿Indeed, we killed﴾ that there was a slain person.

﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾ concerning the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him. For when that event occurred, people differed. Some Jews said: "He was an impostor, so we killed him rightfully." Others were in doubt; some of them said: "If this is Jesus, where is our companion?" Some of them said: "The face is the face of Jesus, and the body is the body of our companion." And one who had heard from him that Allah, the Exalted, would raise him to the heaven said: "He was raised to the heaven." Some people said: "The human nature was crucified and the divine nature ascended."

﴿They are in doubt about it﴾ that is, in hesitation. Doubt is used both for what neither of its two sides is preponderant, and for general hesitation, and for what is opposed to knowledge. Therefore He emphasized it with His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾. The exception is disjunctive, that is, "but they follow assumption." It is permissible to interpret doubt as ignorance, and knowledge as the belief in which the soul finds rest, whether it is certain or otherwise, so the exception is connected.

﴿And they did not kill him for certain﴾ a certain killing, as they claimed by their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah," or while being certain. It is also said its meaning is: what they knew with certainty, like the saying of the poet:

"Thus do the knowing women inform about her, / And indeed I have slain those (doubts) by my knowledge, with certainty."

From their saying: "I killed the thing by knowledge" and "I slaughtered it by knowledge," when you exaggerate in your knowledge of it.

﴿Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself﴾ a refutation and denial of his killing, and an affirmation of his being raised. ﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾ not overcome in what He wills.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 157–158:

﴿And their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah."﴾ That is, according to their claim. It is also possible that they said it mockingly, and its parallel is ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾. It may also be a fresh statement from Allah, the Exalted, praising him, or a placing of a good mention in the place of their foul mention.

﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them.﴾

It is narrated (that a group of Jews insulted him and his mother, so he invoked curses upon them, and Allah transformed them into apes and swine. The Jews then gathered to kill him, so Allah informed him that He would raise him to the heaven. He said to his companions, "Which of you is willing to have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed, crucified, and enters Paradise?" A man from among them stood up, and Allah cast upon him (p-108) his likeness, so he was killed and crucified. And it is said (he was a man who was a hypocrite toward him, who went out to guide them to him, so Allah cast his likeness upon him, and he was seized, crucified and killed), and it is said: (Tituanus the Jew entered a house in which he was, but did not find him, and Allah cast his likeness upon him. When he came out, they thought he was Jesus, so he was seized and crucified). Such things are among the marvels that are not deemed improbable in the time of prophethood. Allah, the Exalted, censured them only for what the discourse indicates of their audacity toward Allah, the Exalted, and their intention to kill His Prophet, who was supported by manifest miracles, and their boasting about it, not for their statement itself, which was according to their assumption. "Was made to appear" is a passive verb with a prepositional phrase as its subject, as if it were said: "rather, the resemblance occurred to them between Jesus and the one killed," or "in the matter," according to the view of one who said: no one was killed, but rumour of his killing spread and circulated among the people; or it refers to the pronoun of the one killed, because of the indication of ﴿Indeed, we killed﴾ that there was a slain person.

﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾ concerning the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him. For when that event occurred, people differed. Some Jews said: "He was an impostor, so we killed him rightfully." Others were in doubt; some of them said: "If this is Jesus, where is our companion?" Some of them said: "The face is the face of Jesus, and the body is the body of our companion." And one who had heard from him that Allah, the Exalted, would raise him to the heaven said: "He was raised to the heaven." Some people said: "The human nature was crucified and the divine nature ascended."

﴿They are in doubt about it﴾ that is, in hesitation. Doubt is used both for what neither of its two sides is preponderant, and for general hesitation, and for what is opposed to knowledge. Therefore He emphasized it with His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾. The exception is disjunctive, that is, "but they follow assumption." It is permissible to interpret doubt as ignorance, and knowledge as the belief in which the soul finds rest, whether it is certain or otherwise, so the exception is connected.

﴿And they did not kill him for certain﴾ a certain killing, as they claimed by their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah," or while being certain. It is also said its meaning is: what they knew with certainty, like the saying of the poet:

"Thus do the knowing women inform about her, / And indeed I have slain those (doubts) by my knowledge, with certainty."

From their saying: "I killed the thing by knowledge" and "I slaughtered it by knowledge," when you exaggerate in your knowledge of it.

﴿Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself﴾ a refutation and denial of his killing, and an affirmation of his being raised. ﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾ not overcome in what He wills.

﴿Wise﴾ in what He arranged for Jesus, peace be upon him.

Verse 159 of Surah an-Nisa' (4): ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾. That is, there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him. His saying "la-yu'minanna bihi" (he will surely believe in him) is an oath clause (جُمْلَةٌ قَسَمِيَّةٌ, *jumla qasamiyya*) that occurs as a descriptive clause (صِفَةً) modifying "aḥad" (anyone). The second pronoun refers back to "aḥad," and the first pronoun refers to Jesus, upon him be peace.

The meaning is: there is none of the Jews and Christians but that he will surely believe that Jesus is the servant of God and His Messenger before he dies, even at the moment his soul is departing. But that faith will not benefit him. This is supported by the reading that has been recited: "illa liyu'minunna bihi qabla mawtihim" (with *liyu'minunna* and *mawtihim*, in the plural), with the *nun* vowelled with a *ḍamma*, because "aḥad" carries the sense of a plural. This is like a warning to them and an exhortation to hasten to faith in him before they are compelled to it, at which point their faith will not benefit them.

It has also been said that both pronouns refer to Jesus, upon him be the best of blessings and peace, and the meaning is: when he descends from the sky, the people of all religions will believe in him.

It is narrated that he, upon him be peace, will descend from the sky when the Dajjal (the false messiah) emerges, and will kill him. No one of the People of the Book will remain but that he will believe in him, until the religion (*milla*) becomes one, which is the religion of Islam. Security will prevail, so that lions will graze with camels, panthers with cattle, and wolves with sheep, and children will play with snakes. He will remain on the earth for forty years, then he will die, the Muslims will pray over him and bury him. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾: he will testify against the Jews that they denied him, and against the Christians that they called him the son of God.

This refers to what He mentioned in His saying (p-109) ﴿And upon those who were Jews We made unlawful﴾. ﴿وَبِصَدِّهِمْ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ كَثِيرًا﴾ means: "And for their hindering from the way of God many," meaning many people, or many instances of hindering.

﴿وَأخْذِهِمُ الرِّبا وقَدْ نُهُوا عَنْهُ﴾ means: "And their taking of usury, though they had been forbidden from it." Usury (ribā) was unlawful for them just as it is unlawful for us. In this is evidence that a prohibition (nahy) indicates unlawfulness (tahrim). ﴿وَأكْلِهِمْ أمْوالَ النّاسِ بِالباطِلِ﴾ means: "And their consuming of people's wealth by falsehood," through bribery and all other unlawful means. ﴿وَأعْتَدْنا لِلْكافِرِينَ مِنهم عَذابًا ألِيمًا﴾ means: "And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment," excluding those who repent and believe.

﴿But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them﴾, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. ﴿And the believers﴾, that is, from among them, or from among the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar). ﴿believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾ is the predicate (khabar, the complement of the subject) of the subject. ﴿And those who establish the prayer﴾ is in the accusative (nusiba) by way of praise (madh), if ﴿believe﴾ is taken as the predicate of "those." Or it is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿what was sent down to you﴾. What is meant by them are the Prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, meaning: they believe in the books and the prophets. It was also recited in the nominative (raf') as coordination with ﴿those firmly grounded﴾, or with the pronoun in ﴿believe﴾, or on the basis that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿those, We shall give them﴾. ﴿And those who give the zakat﴾ is in the nominative according to one of the aforementioned possibilities. ﴿And the believers in God and the Last Day﴾: belief in the Prophets, the books, and following the laws that confirm them is placed before it, because it is the purpose of the verse. ﴿Those, We shall give them a great reward﴾, in return for their combining true faith with righteous deeds. Hamzah recited ﴿sa-yu'tihim﴾ with the letter ya'.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 163:

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him.﴾ This is a reply to the People of the Book regarding their demand that a book be sent down to them from the heavens, and an argument against them that his (ﷺ) case in revelation is like that of the other prophets, upon them be blessings and peace. ﴿And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon.﴾ He singled them out for mention, although the prophets include them, in order to honor them: Abraham is the first of the ulu l-'azm (the Resolute Messengers) among them, and Jesus is the last of them, while the rest are the most noble of the prophets and their most renowned. ﴿And We gave David a Psalter.﴾ Hamzah read "Zabura" with a ḍamma (zabūran), which is the plural of zubur, in the sense of mazbur (that which is written).

**﴿وَرُسُلا﴾** is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb (*mudmar*) indicated by ﴿أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ﴾ ("We revealed to you"), as in the sense of "We sent" (كَأرْسَلْنا), or it is explained by the following: ﴿قَدْ قَصَصْناهم عَلَيْكَ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ ("We have already related them to you before"), meaning before this surah, or before today.

**﴿وَرُسُلا لَمْ نَقْصُصْهم عَلَيْكَ وكَلَّمَ اللَّهُ مُوسى تَكْلِيمًا﴾**: "And messengers We have not related to you. And God spoke to Moses directly." This is the highest level of revelation, and Moses was singled out among them for it. God has, however, favoured Muhammad (ﷺ) by giving him what He gave each one of them.

**﴿رُسُلا مُبَشِّرِينَ ومُنْذِرِينَ﴾**: "Messengers, bearers of good news and warners." The word رُسُلًا is in the accusative either as a term of praise (على المدح), or by an implied verb "We sent" (بإضمار أرسلنا), or as a circumstantial accusative (حال). If it is a circumstantial accusative, رُسُلًا serves as a preparatory term (مُوَطِّئًا) for what follows, like your saying: "I passed by Zayd, a righteous man" (مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ رَجُلًا صالِحًا).

**﴿لِئَلا يَكُونَ لِلنّاسِ عَلى اللَّهِ حُجَّةٌ بَعْدَ الرُّسُلِ﴾**: "So that people will have no argument against God after the messengers." Otherwise they would say: "Why did You not send us a messenger, so he could alert us and teach us what we did not know?" This indicates that the sending of prophets (peace be upon them) to people is a necessity, because all people are unable to grasp the particular details of benefit, and most are unable to grasp its universal principles. The lam (لِ) is connected either to أرسلنا or to the phrase مُبَشِّرِينَ ومُنْذِرِينَ. حُجَّةٌ is the subject of كانَ (يَكُونَ), and its predicate is either لِلنّاسِ or عَلى اللَّهِ, with the other being a circumstantial phrase. It is not permissible for it to be connected to حُجَّةٌ, because it is a verbal noun (مَصْدَرٌ), and بَعْدَ is a temporal adverb (ظَرْفٌ) for it or a qualifier (صِفَةٌ) of it.

**﴿وَكانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا﴾**: "And God is Mighty", meaning He cannot be overcome in what He wills.

**﴿حَكِيمًا﴾**: "Wise", in what He has ordained concerning the matter of prophethood, and He has singled out each prophet with a type of revelation and miracle.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 166:

﴿But Allah bears witness﴾ is an istidrak (a corrective transition) from the implication of what precedes it. It is as if, when they challenged him by demanding a book be sent down to them from heaven, and he argued against them with His saying, ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾, [Allah] said: "They do not bear witness, but Allah bears witness," or [the meaning is]: "They deny it, but Allah confirms it and establishes it." ﴿by what He has sent down to you﴾ refers to the Qur'an, the inimitable [miracle] that indicates your prophethood.

It is narrated that when ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ was revealed, they said: "We do not bear witness for you," and so this was revealed.

﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾: He sent it down accompanied by His own specific knowledge, which is the knowledge of its composition in an arrangement that every eloquent person is unable to match; or [it means] with [knowledge of] the state of one who is prepared for prophethood and worthy of receiving the Book; or with His knowledge of what people need for their livelihood and their hereafter. The prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject on the first two interpretations, and to the object on the third. The sentence serves as an explanation of what precedes it. ﴿And the angels bear witness﴾ likewise to your prophethood. In this there is an indication that they wish to know the truth of the claim to prophethood in a way that dispenses with reflection and contemplation. This kind of knowledge is among the special attributes of the angels (malik), and there is no way for a human being to acquire knowledge of such matters except through thought and reflection. So if these people had applied sound reasoning, they would have recognized your prophethood and borne witness to it, just as the angels recognized it and bore witness. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾: that is, sufficient is what He has established of proofs for the truth of your prophethood, so there is no need to seek testimony from anything else.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verses 167–169:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah have certainly strayed far astray.﴾ Because they combined going astray with leading others astray, and because the one who leads others astray is more deeply immersed in error and further from being rescued from it.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong﴾ [i.e., wrong Muhammad (ﷺ) by denying his prophethood], or [wrong] people by barring them from what is good for them and their salvation, or [it may be understood] in a more general sense than these. The verse indicates that disbelievers are addressed concerning the subsidiary rulings (al-furu', the practical laws), since what is meant by them are those who combine disbelief and wrongdoing. ﴿Allah will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to any path﴾

﴿except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever.﴾ That would be the case, since His prior decree and His inevitable promise stand that whoever dies in his disbelief is an eternal dweller in the Fire; and "abiding" (khalidin) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal muqaddarah), meaning [they will abide there] as a future state. ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ It is not difficult for Him, nor does He regard it as a great matter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 170:

﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord.﴾ Having established the matter of prophethood, and having explained the path that leads to knowledge of it, and the threat against those who deny it, He addressed people in general with the call, the imposition of proof, the promise of reward for accepting, and the threat of punishment for rejecting. ﴿So believe; it is better for you.﴾ That is: believe, (it being) a better belief for you; or: adopt a course better for you than that in which you are. It has also been said that its estimated form is "let faith be better for you" (yakun al-iman khayran lakum), but the Basrans prohibited this, because kana (kāna) is not omitted together with its subject except where it is necessary, and because it leads to the omission of the conditional and its response. ﴿But if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is: and if you disbelieve, then He is Self-Sufficient over you, not harmed by your disbelief just as He is not benefited by your belief. He drew attention to His self-sufficiency by His saying: ﴿to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, and this encompasses what the two contain and what they are composed of.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of their circumstances. ﴿Wise﴾ in what He has arranged for them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 171:

﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess (ghuluww) in your religion.﴾ The address is to both groups. The Jews went to excess in belittling Jesus, peace be upon him, to the point that they accused him of being born out of wedlock, and the Christians went to excess in exalting him, to the point that they took him as a god. It has also been said that the address is to the Christians specifically, since this is more fitting with His words: ﴿and do not say about God except the truth﴾, meaning, declaring Him free of any consort or offspring. ﴿The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is only the Messenger of God and His word which He directed to Mary﴾, meaning, He conveyed it to her and implanted it in her. ﴿And a spirit from Him﴾, meaning, a living being that came forth from Him, not through an intermediary that would serve as a root or material source for him. It has also been said that he was called a spirit because he used to give life to the dead or to hearts. ﴿So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say "Three".﴾ That is, "The gods are three: God, the Messiah, and Mary." This is supported by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?"﴾ Or [the meaning is] ﴿"God is three"﴾, if it is established that they say "God is one of three hypostases (aqanim): the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit," and by "the Father" they mean the essence (dhat), by "the Son" knowledge (ilm), and by "the Holy Spirit" life (hayat). ﴿Desist﴾ from trinitarianism. ﴿It is better for you.﴾ Its accusative case is as explained previously. ﴿God is only one God﴾, meaning, one in essence, with no plurality in Him in any respect. ﴿Glory be to Him that He should have a son﴾, meaning, I glorify Him by declaring Him exalted above having a son, for a son would belong to one who has an equal who resembles him, and would be subject to extinction. ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, in dominion and creation; nothing resembles Him in any of that, so that He would take it as a son. ﴿And sufficient is God as Disposer of affairs﴾, an indication of His independence from a son, for the need for one would be so that he might act as a deputy for his father, while God, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Sustainer who preserves all things, sufficient for that, independent of anyone who might create Him or assist Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 172:

﴿The Messiah will never disdain﴾ will never be too proud, from "nakaftu al-dam'a" (I wiped away the tear), when you remove it with your finger so that its trace is not seen on you. ﴿to be a servant of Allah﴾ from being a servant of Him, for his servitude is an honour in which he takes pride; disdain and humiliation lie only in serving other than Him.

It is narrated: "The delegation of Najran said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: Why do you disparage our companion? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Who is your companion? They said: Jesus, peace be upon him. He ﷺ said: And what should I say? They said: You say that he is the servant of Allah and His messenger. He said: It is no disgrace for him to be a servant of Allah. They said: Indeed (it is not)." Then it was revealed.

﴿Nor the angels, those brought near﴾ is a conjunction with "the Messiah," i.e., nor do the angels brought near disdain to be servants of Allah. Those who claim the superiority of the angels over the prophets, peace be upon them, have cited this. It is said that the context of the verse is to refute the Christian position that raises the Messiah above the station of servitude, and this requires that the conjoined be higher in rank than the one it is conjoined to, so that the non-disdain of the angels serves as evidence for the non-disdain of the Messiah. Its answer is that the verse is a refutation of those who worship the Messiah and the angels, so this does not hold; and even if its restriction to the Christians is granted, perhaps he intended the conjunction as hyperbole in terms of multiplicity, not magnitude, like your saying: "The commander has risen; no chief or subordinate opposes him." And if he intended magnitude, its furthest implication is the superiority of the angels brought near, who are the Cherubim surrounding the Throne, or those of higher rank among the angels, over the Messiah among the prophets, peace be upon them all; and that does not necessitate the superiority of one of the two kinds over the other absolutely, and the dispute concerns this.

﴿And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant﴾ and whoever rises above it. Istikbar (arrogance) is less than istinkaf (disdain), and for this reason it is conjoined to it. Istikbar is used where there is no entitlement, unlike takabbur (haughtiness), which may be by entitlement.

﴿He will gather them to Himself all together﴾ then He will recompense them.

Verse 173 of Surah an-Nisa' (4): "As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty. But as for those who disdain and are arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find for themselves besides Allah no protector or helper."

This is an elaboration (tafsil) of the general recompense (al-mujazah al-'ammah) that is indicated by the import (fahwa) of the discourse. It is as if He said: "He will gather them all to Himself on the Day when He gathers the servants for recompense, or for the recompense of their deeds." For rewarding those who are opposed to them and bestowing favour upon them is itself a punishment for them, through grief and regret.

﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalala (a person who dies without ascendants or descendants)﴾. Its interpretation has already been explained at the beginning of the surah.

﴿If a man dies leaving no child, and he has a sister, she has half of what he left﴾. The word امْرُؤٌ (imru'un, "a man") is in the nominative case (ارْتَفَعَ), governed by a verb that is explained by the apparent verb, namely هَلَكَ (halaka, "dies"). The phrase لَيْسَ لَهُ ولَدٌ (laysa lahu walad, "has no child") is either a descriptive qualifier (صِفَة) of imru'un or a circumstantial clause (حال, ḥāl) referring to the hidden pronoun (المُسْتَكِنّ) in هَلَكَ. The و in وَلَهُ may be taken as a circumstantial marker (الحال) or as a conjunction (العَطْف). The sister here means the full sister (from both parents) or the half-sister from the father, because her brother is made an agnatic heir (عَصَبَة, 'aṣaba), and the son of the mother cannot be an agnatic heir. The word walad is to be taken in its apparent meaning. Although the sister inherits alongside a daughter according to the majority of scholars, unlike Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, she does not inherit half.

﴿And he inherits her﴾: that is, a man inherits his sister, if the situation is reversed. ﴿If she has no child﴾, whether male or female. If the phrase yarithuha ("he inherits her") is understood to mean that he inherits all of her property, then this applies; otherwise, the intended meaning is a male child, since a daughter does not exclude a brother. The verse, just as it does not indicate that brothers are excluded by someone other than a child, also does not indicate that they are not excluded by a child. The Sunnah has indicated that they do not inherit alongside the father, and likewise the implication of His words, ﴿Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalala﴾, if kalala is interpreted as referring to the deceased.

﴿If there are two sisters, they have two-thirds of what he left﴾. The pronoun refers to those who inherit through siblinghood, and the dual form is treated according to meaning. The purpose of describing them with the dual (اثْنَتَيْنِ,ithnatayn, "two") is to draw attention to the fact that the ruling is based on number, regardless of their youth, age, or other conditions.

﴿And if they are brothers and sisters, men and women, the male has the share of two females﴾. Its original form is: "And if they are brothers and sisters," but the masculine was given precedence (فَغَلَبَ المُذَكَّرُ).

﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾: that is, Allah makes clear to you your error, which is inherent in you when you are left to yourselves and your natures, so that you may guard against it and seek its opposite. Or, Allah makes clear to you the truth and the right course, out of disliking that you go astray. It is said that the meaning is "lest you go astray," with the particle lā (لا) omitted, and this is the view of the Kufan grammarians (الكُوفِيِّينَ, al-Kūfiyyīn).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾. So He knows the welfare of His servants in life and in death.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Nisa', it is as if he has given charity to every believing man and believing woman, he inherits an inheritance, he is given a reward like one who frees a slave, he is cleared of shirk, and he is among those whom Allah, the Exalted, may pardon, if He wills."
